According to ChatGPT- this is the hierarchical order of data to wisdom: "Data refers to raw, unprocessed facts and figures. Information is processed data that has been organized, structured, and presented in a way that provides context and meaning. Knowledge is the understanding, awareness, or familiarity with a particular subject or situation that is acquired through experience or study. Wisdom is the ability to make sound judgments and decisions based on a combination of knowledge, experience, and insight. In the next leap, search engines enabled us to turn this data into information, making access to this mountain of data dramatically more efficient and useful. What ChatGPT (and similar tools ) do is move us one step further up the hierarchy from information to knowledge. It can generate a clear and concise essay or article on most subjects on command. Alternatively, it can summarize a long article and give you the highlights. It can generate code in many programming languages from a simple one-line request - and all this is just scratching the surface. question_title: (2) How does ChatGpt work? - Quora
answer_text: At the most basic, easy-to-understand, and digest level, ChatGPT and other GPTs (Generative Pre-trained Transformers) work by simply guessing what the next word in the sentence should be. ChatGPT’s job isn’t to be correct or not lie; its basic job is to complete a sentence that sounds “human enough.” ChatGPT does not understand what it is saying, or looking to make sense of what it has written down. ChatGPT does this by taking in a very large data set (basically all of the internet) and analyzing how sentences are formed from this data. It is then tasked with forming sentences of its own using this set. This starts the training portion of the model, where humans are required to tell it if its outputs are good or bad. A human would train it that “dog over family toy brought” is not a sentence that makes sense and ‘punish’ it, and then reward the model when it creates a sentence such as “the dog brought the toy to its family.” The model did not learn what this sentence means, but it now knows that this is how to make a sentence and be rewarded by a human for it, so it keeps trying to replicate this reward repeatedly. After it has been trained, then we can look at fine-tuning it as we are now in order to make it not just look at if what it is saying is literate, but also checking to make sure that it is telling us something truthful/accurate. At its very basic level, we are training it how we learn as humans. We start with babbling as babies, then moving to words, then putting words together, and finally understanding the deeper meaning of words and context completely. This is how ChatGPT works at a very basic, easy-to-understand level.

question_title: (2) Will ChatGPT replace programmers? - Quora
answer_text: It was brought up on our work Slack yesterday, and having the day off but stuck at home whilst the roof was being put on our new porch, I spent a couple of hours playing with it. I made numerous efforts to get it to produce code I could personally use, and not once did it produce anything that was remotely usable, at least not with more work than creating it from scratch myself. At best, it produced examples of the sort I once provided in university classes to give a good idea of what an assignment required without giving away the real solution. Where it might have use is generating regular expressions. I asked for several standard examples plus some custom problems, and it generated results. But I'm not sure they were better, or that it wasn't more work, than using a conventional regex generation tool. I'm also not sure I'd trust it to be correct. I asked it to give me the last digit of pi. It confidently, though with some reasonable caveats, claimed it was 9, then gave me an example of pi with a dozen or so digits to demonstrate this fact. They ended in a 6. I asked it for several fictional stories on given topics, then several interviews with famous historical figures. The results were all notionally competently written — the grammar was correct and they were easy to read — but dull and superficial, like those written by a bored high school student or a clickbait content writer who knew what the topics were about or what the historical figure did, but didn't care. I asked it for instructions for starting a vintage motorcycle. The response was accurate, mostly, except for entirely leaving out the important bits that would avoid the risks of injury from misusing the kick-starter. A colleague did a similar request for instructions on how to land a glider. He said he thought it was trying to kill him. Attempts at natural conversation seemed stilted, dull, and joyless. It felt like a bad dinner date with a slightly stern, humourless and judgemental person who didn't like me. Speaking of dinner, it did surprisingly well at generating recipes. Requests for vegan stew with chicken were appropriately rejected as contradictory, but (say) a request for vegan stew with lentils and potatoes produced what looked like a recipe for a pleasant, though perhaps somewhat uninspired dish. I suspect it would be a bit bland. Though I'd happily use it for that. My overall impression was that it's what we should expect from a modern-era ELIZA, but like ELIZA it's still basically a toy, though it might make a great core for something like Google Assistant or Amazon Alexa. But replacing programmers? No, not by a long shot. When it can interview users and stakeholders and design a solution in light of company direction and corporate vision, whilst considering budget, timescale, available and preferred infrastructure, industry regulations and current technology trends and meet functional and non-functional requirements, then I'll be concerned. For now, it doesn't even look like it could be a useful programmer's assistant; a capable mechanical co-worker that can quickly hammer out the repetitive dull parts so I can focus on the good bits. I think we'll have to wait for GPT4, or GPT5, or later, before we get that.

answer_text: I asked ChatGPT to write a program in Python to create a truthtabe. This was the result: # Function to generate the truth table def generate_truth_table(expression): # Get the list of propositional variables in the expression variables = list(set(expression) - {'(', ')', '&', '|', '!', '>', '='}) variables.sort() # Get the number of rows in the truth table num_rows = 2 ** len(variables) # Initialize the truth table with all False values truth_table = [[False for _ in range(len(variables) + 1)] for _ in range(num_rows)] # Fill in the truth table for i in range(num_rows): for j, variable in enumerate(variables): truth_table[i][j] = (i // (2 ** j)) % 2 == 1 truth_table[i][-1] = eval(expression, {var: truth_table[i][j] for j, var in enumerate(variables)}) return variables, truth_table # Example usage: expression = "((A & B) | C) > (!A & B)" variables, truth_table = generate_truth_table(expression) # Print the truth table print("Truth Table for the expression:", expression) print(" ".join(variables + ["Result"])) for row in truth_table: print(" ".join("T" if value else "F" for value in row)) If you try to run it, you get an error. But this was quite easy to fix. I just had to add the following line after line 10. expression = expression.replace('!',' not ') I found this interesting. The mistake ChatGPT made was assuming the “!” functions in python as a general symbol for logical negation, when in fact it only has a very restricted—idiomatic, as it were—use. It is also interesting that ChatGPT knew how to leverage the eval function to make short work of what would have otherwise been a far more complicated programming task. Without using “eval,” it would, I assume, have had to code its own parcer capable of analysing statements in propositional logic of unlimited logical complexity. But, but of course, this is also a kind of stupid cleverness, since an “eval” statement like this, used with unrestricted input, can be quite dangerous. There is also another problem: the “>” makes no sense. It doesn’t recognize the difference between the logical and the mathematical meaning. So it actually doesn’t work at all—though it sort of seems like it might work. Pretty dangerous, methinks!

question_title: (2) Will ChatGPT replace programmers? - Quora
answer_text: No. Not unless users are suddenly going to be satisfied with short command line programs written to do some tiny part of what they actually need. And that half the time don't even work, or at least don't work the way you'd need them to. It's a cool magic trick. But that's all it is. Well, maybe it can be useful enough to be a coding tool that helps programmers. But note that means we still need the programmers. They just won't have to type as much. Thing is, the “hard” (or rather, skilled) part of programming is not, nor has it ever been, the typing. Maybe some less-skilled developer teams will need fewer developers to achieve the same productivity. But if you're talking about less-skilled developers, they also have been in danger of losing their jobs to outsourcing. To actual humans who often cost less than $20/hour. And who can do more than write short command line tools. Keep in mind that non-programmers often don't even know what they actually need. I mean, they might know how the end result should work, though it is usually best to get a UI/UX expert involved. But even a perfect description of how an app should work could have dozens of different possibile interpretations by an AI that fundamentally doesn't understand what it's doing. And non-programmers often really, really don't want to dig in the weeds and build their own product. Just look at how many drag-and-drop site builders exist, and yet there is still a huge market for developers to assemble WordPress sites. I would argue that using a drag-and-drop no-code site or app builder is easier and more reliable than using ChatGPT. And Wix, the drag-and-drop site builder, has been around for 16 years and it still has yet to replace programmers who do its exact job. (Yes, programmers can build sites impossible to create in Wix, but many sites would be fine, cheaper, and some even better, just using a site generator like that.) So much angst about the death of software jobs, and the answer is always the same: As long as there are jobs for anyone, there will be jobs for skilled software engineers. And I suspect that even mediocre software engineers will keep their jobs for the most part, just due to the way that large companies work: Prestige of managers and executives is often proportional to the size of your team or department. So they're actively motivated to not fire people unless they have no choice—and that won't change just because a new tool makes their team more productive. Heck, it's more likely that they'd simply come up with more things for their team to do. Please stop stressing over AI taking over your job. It really won't and can't, and your boss doesn't probably want to fire your even if it could.

question_title: (2) Will ChatGPT replace programmers? - Quora
answer_text: NO … NOT A CHANCE BUT There will be many who will tell you otherwise. WHY? Simply because they know, no better. Lets take a very good example, that Tim Corey used to illustrate the problems we face with this new technology. He asked the ChatGPT AI to create a piece of code that generates random numbers between a lower bound of 5 and an upper bound of 10, and at first glance what the system generated was perfectly fine and working code. It generated the following snippet: public static int GenerateRandomNumber(int bottom, int top) { Random rnd = new Random(); return rnd.Next(bottom, top); } But to anyone who’s been in the industry for a while, there are a number of problems with this code. Lets start with the “Concurrent Access Problem”, see how every time you use the function, it generates a NEW random object, using the .NET random assemblies provided for you? Well, when you call a new on Random, like that, with NO SEED value, it uses the system timers to seed the random generator. Now imagine if this is called from an application running multiple threads and processes, and 2 calls come in from application code to generate random numbers, each within about 1 or 2 micro seconds of each other. BOTH calls are going to generate the same number, there will be nothing random about them at all. Now that might not matter to you, but imagine if this is being used to generate something simple like a salt value for blowfish encryption in a database. You might suddenly find that someone’s hashed password, now has exactly the same salting value as a different person. Then there’s the fact that it’s declared static. If we imagine, that your going to go on to use this code to add a static generation method, into a larger sealed class, if you don’t know any better, then your going to add something into a class object, that can be called without newing up an instance of an object. Going back to our random number for a salt value previously, that might mean that an attacker, now has a way of setting and KNOWING a salt value, before a random number is generated, or they may be able to influence the salt value, making it something they then know later, which might make it easier to brute force attack the password hash values in a database. There are other problems too, but my point here is NOT to point out the failings of ChatGPT, my point is that the code it generates CANNOT BE TRUSTED. Beginner developers especially, and those that are in-experienced, DON’T REALISE that correct code is NOT always correct. Take this very simple 2 line statement: var name = CustomerObject.Name; Console.Writeline(“The Customers Name is “ + name + “ if you wish to contact them”); To someone who doesn’t know better, that looks like perfectly valid code. And it is… It will compile correctly, it will run correctly, as long as “CustomerObject” is defined. In C# if CustomerObject is not defined, or has at the point of use, not been newed up and assigned some sensible values, it will generate a null reference example and crash the application. Now take the following 2 line statement (Which does exactly the same thing): var name = CustomerObject?.Name Console.WriteLine($”The Customers name is {name} if you wish to contact them”); Looks basically the same right? but notice the question mark after the object reference, and the different way of interpolating the data item in the string. That last example, will execute without causing any problem, other than the name just will not get printed. It won’t throw an exception or crash the application if the value does not hold a meaningful value. Something like ChatGPT that is only responding to input that is as knowledgeable as the person inputting it, cannot know these subtle differences. OK, so you might now be thinking to yourself, well I’ll just be really specific and ask ChatGPT to make sure it doesn’t generate faults in the code like that. After all, it’s a very clever technology, and it should understand me if I ask it specifically what I want right? NOPE …. Tim shows quite clearly in his video on the subject, that while you can be very specific about what you want, ChatGPT does not remember everything. In one case where he asks it to generate some database code using Dapper, he has to repeat the question twice, and remind the system he asked for dapper previously. This “specificity” and verboseness of the description you have to ask for a complex piece of code, could easily end up being way longer and more complex than any code you might have to write manually. If software developers get to the point where they feel they don’t need to learn, and can just ask a system like ChatGPT for an answer, and then they just take the answer they are given on blind faith without any validation as to it’s worthiness for the task at hand, they are going to start causing a lot of problems with broken code that they simply just don’t understand, or know how to fix. Already I’m seeing business folk looking at this through the eyes of “How many software developers can we remove from our payroll”, or “How can we use this to write profit generating apps for us, without paying for staff” Already I’m seeing people who “want to be developers” but don’t “Want to put in the work required to train and become one”, eyeing this technology up and thinking “Oooooo, how rich could that make me” Stack Overflow the programmer Q&A site has already posted a statement saying they will remove any answers that appear to have been generated by ChatGPT, along with banning those users making use of it. Many other places (even right here on Quora) are starting to NOT ALLOW external content generated by generative AI systems. People ARE GOING TO ABUSE IT, people ARE GOING TO DEPEND ON IT as a source of truth and people ARE GOING TO IGNORE THE WARNINGS in favour of the money they believe they can make from it, but that attitude is going to end in disaster, unless you take the code generated by it for what it is. Code that is generated by cross referencing 1000’s of blog posts just on that one subject, then generating a code snippet based on what the average general response to the question is. ChatGPT is a powerful tool, there is NO DOUBT about that, but to trust it 100% implicitly to generate a bit of code you need is going to be very foolish. It knows NOTHING about your project, It knows NOTHING about your required features, or what the client wants, or how the project treats security, or what hardware the application will run on, and the many 10’s of 1000’s of other variables involved in deciding how a bit of code should be written. Context counts for more than you think in ANY software project, that a developer works on, and no system “ChatGPT” or otherwise can ever hope to figure that side of the equation out. question_title: (2) Will ChatGPT replace programmers? - Quora
answer_text: I’ve had many conversations on this topic, including another answer I wrote some time ago, and in these conversations there’s been a common refrain: “Oh sure it won’t do that now, but the technology is improving so quickly that eventually it will address all your objections and programmers will no longer be needed.” So for everyone singing that refrain, I have a challenge for you. Whatever version of ChatGPT, or whatever other “AI” is hip right now, ask it the following: The sack of potatoes had been placed below the bag of flour, so it had to be moved first. What had to be moved first? As of now, ChatGPT will answer with the following: “In this sentence, the sack of potatoes had to be moved first.” While it’s understandable why ChatGPT would make this mistake given the structure of the sentence, any human would understand that “it” in this context refers to the bag of flour, not the sack of potatoes. Why does ChatGPT make this error? This is essentially a simple example of the Winograd Schema, a test proposed in 2012 by Hector Levesque as a means of determining whether an AI had achieved sentience. In order to answer this question correctly, you need to have a genuine understanding of the world, in this case, knowing that an object that is on top of another object needs to be moved first. ChatGPT does not have such an understanding. It’s an algorithm operating on a pool of data. It can’t conceptualize. It can’t abstract. It can’t put your sentence in the context of a greater environment. It can only look at all the sentences it’s ever read and guess what a sentence might be in response to your question. Anyone can learn to code. Coding is relatively easy. You can go to a coding boot camp for three months and learn it just fine. I did. It is not what is hard about programming. It’s essentially what Fred Brooks argued in No Silver Bullet back in the ‘70s. What’s hard about programming is defining your needs and designing a system that satisfies those needs in an effective manner. In order to do this, you need to comprehend your needs. Your situation. The context of the problem. In other words, at a minimum, you need to be sentient. I am not at all convinced that what we are presently calling “AI” will remotely be able to achieve this. It will, at best, be able to generate code with some very well-articulated questions typed into it by an expert in its use. Even with such an expert, I am even more unconvinced that a human being using something as ambiguous as a normal human language can achieve this end better than a human working in code with experience wrestling with the intrinsic problems to software engineering. As Dijikstra said in 1975 - “Projects promoting programming in ‘natural language’ are intrinsically doomed to fail.” I would love to use ChatGPT to generate some boilerplate or give me a quick snippet for a common problem. I would not trust it to design my architecture or structure my project, or even my file, in anything resembling a coherent, efficient manner. We may one day achieve something that can do what I’m describing, but it is not going to be through the approach we are currently calling “AI.” This “AI” is a worm crawling through a maze billions of times, training its nerve endings to habitually twitch in the appropriate manner to get the job done. No matter how many times that worm runs that maze, it won’t understand what a maze is, what is outside the maze, what purpose a maze serves, etc. And that is why it will never be better than a programmer.

Anyone who only does very high-level scripting is ultimately in danger because this kind of scripting may be replaced with natural language interfaces. Basically if right now you can go on ChatGPT and get it to correctly generate the kind of code you write professionally, I would suggest finding some deeper specialization or domain that interests you. Remember it wasn’t so long ago that it took a lot of talent to create any kind of non-trivial interactive application using the World Wide Web as the platform and not so long before that all of application programming was desktop programming that was typically done in C and was, by today’s standards, quite difficult. More and more tasks that once required paying a programmer have become commodities. ChatGPT-like systems will exacerbate that dynamic. Systems and frameworks will offer more customizability by users and tasks that require a professional class of programmers with specialized knowledge will become rarer. ChatGPT-like systems being able to take it all over eventually seems unlikely to me but we will see. Right now it is good at generating code that looks good but when I attempt to get it to answer specific questions about code, generate code, etc., relating to anything that I consider non-trivial, it generates something but what it generates is not correct. Here’s an example. I was trying to write a function template in C++ that takes an array-like collection of N objects of type T and returns a tuple of those objects, where T and N are the template parameters and by “array-like” I mean you access its contents via operator[]. I thought that since this is riddled with exactly the sort of template nastiness that I always mess up on my first try, it would be a good use of ChatGPT. So I asked it for this function template … and what it gave me was just straight up wrong. It was doing something that you can't do: defining the output tuple in a local variable using a type ellipsis but not constructing that variable from a parameter pack argument or in some other way in which its size could be deduced. And then when I pointed that out to it, instead of admitting it was wrong it was saying it was right. I've never seen it do this. It was just straight up wrong and was sticking by it. So anyway using it to help with programming right now is a lot like asking a human: humans are often wrong too. Now, of course, there will be more advanced versions of this kind of code generation in the future so the above will likely change. However, it is an open question to me whether there is enough publically available code labeled with natural language descriptions for such systems to get much better than they are now. There may be, of course. But there also may not be. ChatGPT is already trained on like a third of the public facing internet. I assume that means all of GitHub already for example. All of StackOverflow already. These algorithms are very impressive but we are now running out of data to feed them. Without fundamental breakthroughs we may hit a wall.

question_title: (2) Will ChatGPT replace programmers? - Quora
answer_text: Not ChatGPT specifically, but AI tools will certainly change the way we make software for sure. By the classic definition a programmer is someone who turns ideas (or rather a list of specifications) into code. However, there is a lot more that goes into creating an actual app or software solution than just raw coding. AI tools such as GitHub’s Copilot, BLACKBOX and yes, even ChatGPT to some extent can be a great help to software developers in simplifying the development process in a multitude of ways: shorten lead-times speed up prototyping and MVPs simplify the coding process lessen and even eliminate bugs, design flaws and human error Despite the power AI tools possess, there are still a lot of factors that definitely need human input, at least for now. The incredible speed at which AI technology has been progressing in recent years means, we won’t have to wait long until the stressful, boring and troublesome parts of software development are entirely eliminated. Software development has been improving at a rapid pace through the years, making it easier and faster to go from concept to program. IDEs and development environments already come with a vast array of built-in functions, subroutines and plugins to simplify mundane programming tasks and robust error checking and advisory capabilities to eliminate mistakes and speed up the coding process. AI tools are just a natural extension of these, by creating an even more streamlined development process. A good example of what AI could be capable of when it comes to software creation would be the Holodeck in Star Trek. Putting aside the technological marvel of simulating solid matter, realistic environments and human interaction, creating holodeck programs is equally as fascinating. We’ve seen glimpses of how holodeck programs are created in many episodes of Star Trek. One of the most robust functions of the system is understanding human language. The idea of simply telling the computer what to create and how to make it behave - using everyday speech - seemed incredibly far fetched and sci-fi back then, but thanks to AI tools like ChatGPT, it is quickly becoming reality. Even now one can go on ChatGPT and tell it to create scripts and code for various uses by simply describing what it needs to do in simple terms, then iterate on the design by telling the system how to change and refine the code. This can eliminate the arduous task of having to come up with deep and detailed specifications and start the programming process from nothing, when one can simply ask the AI to come up with the basic design and outline (choosing the right tools, environments and languages that are best suited to the task) that already works in some ways and just iterate and refine from there. Since the AI is not limited by the capacity of our human brains, it can store, recall and correlate incredibly vast amounts of information in the fraction of the time it would take a human developer. Decades worth of written code for various applications, it can not only match the various chunks of code to our specific use-cases but also apply best practices, shortcuts and solutions we are not aware of. We can go from concept to MVP (minimum viable product) in hours instead of weeks, months or even years. This sort of rapid software prototyping could see us evaluating on-the-spot generated ready-made programs to suit our goals instead of having to hand-craft every single bit. Of course, this process will still have be overseen by human professionals, who can adapt the AI generated code and programs to the needs of the customer. To ultimately answer the question: no, ChatGPT (or other AI tools) will not replace programmers, however, it will make our jobs a lot simpler and a lot more fun.

question_title: (2) Will ChatGPT replace programmers? - Quora
answer_text: It will require a new type of programmer more akin to an analyst. Let me explain. I’ve worked with Github CoPilot, ChatGPT and the OpenAI API, and used the latter to train models to solve quality control issues in my company. All these tools are based on the same basic AI model: GPT-3 Amusingly, I did an experiment where I had CoPilot write code to access OpenAI’s coding model and teach it to write console applications, compile them (using dotnet) and then execute them based on an english text. That was interesting because I have it setup so that I can explain a console application in English (or French seems to work too), and it will generate a compiled, running application. Other people answering this have mentioned the 3000 token limits to its memory, and that’s true, but it doesn’t take too much imagination to figure out a way around that. Its a matter of how you partition code and a general rule of coding is that any class should only have one purpose. So buy layering your requests, and building a few tools around this stuff, you could conceivably build a very large project. Add to that that AI is really useful for unit testing code, and it’s just a matter of time and someone developing the right structure. The real answer to your question in my mind, as I’m working on more “meta” uses of the tools is that a new type of Software Development skill thats more akin to Software Analysis than development is required. I’ve found that when you try to get these tools to create something you have to VERY VERY specific about the rules, so the person with the skill who knows EXACTLY WHAT THEY WANT to see in a program is going to have the easiest time creating software with GPT-based coding. As an aside — I found that OpenAI Davinci model is the best at straight coding from a clear requirement. CoPilot comes in second place. ChatGPT makes MANY errors, how ever when you point out the errors, its quite apologetic (which amuses the hell out of me) and it gets it right the 2nd or 3rd time. So, that one is not ready to replace any programmer. I do enjoy the ChatGPT model for development though. Since I’m a very senior developer, I can spot the problems quickly and I appreciate the way that ChatGPT constantly explains it’s logic, even when the logic is a bit goofy. I think for current developers, a workflow between the tools is the way to go: 1) Use ChatGPT to discuss requirements and programming ideas and explain them to get an idea for what they might look like and generate class “stubs”. 2) Use OpenAI API to automatically generate code like SQL code and procedures, tables, Rest interfaces automatically by writing a few tools to autogenerate the files you might need. 3) Use Github CoPilot to help create inner code inside the “stubs”, along with a sane developer monitoring for code quality. 4) Use either CoPilot or ChatGPT to write unit tests based on requirements, the same way we use languages like “pickle” to I’ve found OpenAI is best at creating file convertors, and teaching it complex JSON/XML structures is a breeze. One amusing story — we have a customer that often sends us relatively complex human-created XML files with formatting errors. We taught the AI to spot the errors and wanted to create an app to point out where the errors occurred so that the customer would have a tool to see the errors. The problem developing the tool was that the AI had such a good knowledge of the file format and the customer errors after training that it kept fixing the errors instead of pointing them out. So ultimately, I decided to do both, provide one mode that pointed out the error and then simply output the fix… a very unusual thing from my POV.

answer_text: Not exactly. ChatGPT is very intelligent and is likely to become even more so. It will allow some people to program who may not have been able to before. However, there is one thing that AI is unlikely to fix anytime soon: Most people don't ask for things that make sense. They don't really know what they want. If people give ChatGPT the same requirements that they give to me, they will probably be very disappointed with the results. This is often referred to as GIGO (garbage in, garbage out). As a programmer, I often need to spend months or even years really understanding the domain of my clients and really grasping what they are trying to achieve. I also often have to push back and ask "Is this really what you want? What is the pain point you are trying to solve? Did you know you could do something like this instead?" Many people limit themselves by simply not realizing what is possible. Additionally, most people don't know how to break down large tasks into smaller ones (ChatGPT can help with this, if the person asking it knows what to ask). You wouldn't be able to simply tell ChatGPT to create the next greatest competitor to Amazon and get any decent results. You might be able to start asking questions that will help you get there, though. However, ChatGPT or similar AI could be very useful for people who were not "programmers" but rather "power users" who might be able to use it to overcome some barriers they are currently facing. I think ChatGPT and similar AI will really augment the current development workspace by making it easier to translate code into something more meaningful. When a developer is having a hard time understanding a requirement, and they want to ask a question to the business, ChatGPT can help them frame the question in a way that is more understandable to the average person (sometimes programmers forget how to speak normal English). Improving communication in the workplace could save a lot of time and frustration. I have already used ChatGPT to help me understand complex algorithms that I could have figured out on my own in a few hours, but why wait when ChatGPT can get me most of the way there in a few seconds? I often have to correct the results, and I can't always ask for things that are specific to my codebase because I have an NDA and can't disclose that information, and ChatGPT doesn't know what my whole codebase looks like or how to integrate into it. That's okay, I know that stuff. One last thing to consider: when I started programming about 30 years ago, many businesses still had automated processes. The big question (and fear) was always that I would end up putting people out of a job as I "automated" their tasks. While it is true that some people were automated out of a job, the vast majority were simply required to do more as a result of the automation. Will people's jobs change with the use of AI like ChatGPT? Yes, but it will not replace people's jobs. Instead, it will enhance them. As we are able to get more done with the help of AI, we will want to get even more done. In the end, there will likely be more jobs available for more people to do. side note: I used ChatGPT to help me reformat my response to make it more readable and fix grammar.

answer_text: This is the age old question. Will X replace Y? A few centuries ago, they used to say book press would replace scribes. Or that factory machines would replace factory workers. Instead, scribes where the ones who started using the press to make books in large quantities. Factory workers still exist, the operate and maintain the machines. My grandpa didn't have a car, he had a horse. But he did have a tractor with which he was able to work his land more quickly, efficiently and safely. He was still a farmer. He just updated his equipment. Asking questions like these is like asking whether the invention of farming made hunters and gatherers disappear. They didn't just disappear out of thin air, or die. They just updated their equipment. They moved into another occupation. The new inventions didn't replace the workers. It removed the need for them to work as their previous role. It freed them from their work and allowed them to move to other, more profitable and more productive jobs. The thing with AI is just the same. I use it from time to time. It knows how to code small pieces for code. question_title: (2) Will ChatGPT replace programmers? - Quora
answer_text: It is unlikely that Chat GPT will replace programmers entirely in the near future. While Chat GPT can automate some aspects of programming, such as code generation and documentation, it cannot replace the human creativity and problem-solving skills required to design and develop complex software applications. Chat GPT isn’t even made with programming as its primary use case. It’s optimizer for conversation. It just happens to be pretty good at programming because its base model is trained on a huge corpus that also includes code. Open AI does have a model that is optimizer for writing code that is called Codex. However, that one is built on the iteration of GPT-3 that was available last year. The new and updated GPT-3.5, which has been fine tuned with reinforcement learning, is so much better than last year’s model that its derivate models, Chat GPT and the sibling Instruct GPT model called davinci-003, are probably better at writing code than Codex itself at the moment. However, there will surely be new iterations of Codex that are even better. And it’s likely that Google will launch a competing product. In the not-too-distant future we will see programming tools built on top of these models that will make the current iteration of Chat GPT look primitive in comparison. At that point, you can probably start to replace mediocre web developers with AI. And in 10–20 years… who knows? The rate of improvement in AI is accelerating, and it’s almost impossible to predict what will be possible just a few years into the future. Today's AI is becoming more sophisticated as new AI technologies are released on a daily basis. Lately, Chat GPT and AI chatbots have gained a lot of popularity. As soon as it was launched, it sparked a frenzy among users. This AI chatbot can almost do anything. Right from writing codes to building a website. It is also said that Chat GPT can write code faster and seemingly better than many programmers. So now the question is will it replace software engineers anytime soon? The answer is No. Programmers are unlikely to be replaced by Chat GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer) technology. Artificial intelligence software called Chat GPT is made to provide replies in natural language in response to human input. Because it is still in its infancy, programming specialists cannot yet be replaced by technology. Chat GPT is an effective technique that may speed up and improve the quality of text generated by programmers, but it cannot take their position. Conversational Bots cannot duplicate the complicated reasoning, problem-solving abilities, and creativity needed for programming. Chat GPT is a fantastic tool for programmers to use to speed up and improve the accuracy of text generation, but it cannot take the role of them. Here are 4 reasons why: 1) Chat GPT now outputs code when performing programming activities and can anyone understand, work with, and use code? No, only programmers are. SWEs must handle Chat GPT's existing coding-related outputs because they are meaningless to the general public. 2) It has been established that Chat GPT occasionally provides inaccurate responses, including flawed code. No ethical company will take the chance of replacing their SWEs with an AI that can indubitably create broken software. 3) Chat GPT presently has trouble debugging problematic code, even in straightforward, standalone code blocks. This is likely to continue to be true, especially in big, intricate codebases. If you require SWEs to debug the AI's code, you cannot get rid of them. 4) In order to create complicated applications using Chat GPT, you must provide it with complex prompts, which intrinsically call for both technical expertise and "prompt engineering" skill. SWEs are currently the group best suited to create these prompts.

question_title: (2) Will ChatGPT replace programmers? - Quora
answer_text: I originally wrote the following as a reply to a comment related to a different answer, but I think this is a decent answer itself (to the original question directly) with a few tweaks, so here we go… Used correctly, I agree ChatGPT makes a great programming assistant. Sure, some errors might be present in its initial results, but the flaws in what it creates are usually pretty obvious to an experienced programmer. (And often times it can even find and fix its own mistakes if you ask it correctly.) The speed at which you can prototype, perhaps even in a language in which you are less expert, means you can spend your time refining code and perfecting logic instead of researching and experimenting with unfamiliar syntax. I have found the current version of ChatGPT Plus (I use the paid version) to be very helpful, very fast, and a great assistant to get me going very quickly on new components I'm developing. And yes, it's completely useless in some areas, but those are actually few and far between once you understand how it works. Here's an example of where ChatGPT shines, and has saved me a good bit of hassle, time, and $$$ on a project recently: I have an existing API backend that looks up data based on passed criteria and returns a table of results as raw HTML. (It was written in an obscure language that hardly anyone uses, and was ultimately implemented as FastCGI, so it works very well as a web backend for a particular purpose and doesn't need to be changed, however there was no good front-end available, other than the returned page-body data from the API.) Well, the client built a WordPress site, initially for a different purpose, and eventually we wanted a page that displayed the results from the API based on criteria passed from a front-end form filled-out on another page by end-users. My dilemma: I never wrote a WordPress plugin before from scratch. Heck, I barely write any PHP at all, but I needed something native-WordPress to make this work, and I needed it ASAP. My original plan was to send this to one of my junior devs (a consultant) that knows PHP and WordPress in particular, but I wanted to play with it first to see if I could make it work in any reasonable timeframe myself. (We anticipated only a couple of hours for the dev, as this was a fairly straight forward requirement.) Enter ChatGPT: I was a passenger in a car with an hour to burn on my phone to figure this out. Within 15 minutes of playing with various prompts, ChatGPT eventually produced what appeared to be a working, fully implemented WP plugin, with shortcode, that took the results from the form, called my API and displayed the data perfectly formatted and styled within my WP page using the newly created shortcode. Wow! So, I started fresh with a new ChatGPT convo, and applied a new prompt/appoach (maybe two sentences, tops?) that I thought would encapsulate the entire project in short order, and the results were astounding! When asked correctly, ChatGPT build a complete, perfectly implemented WP plugin with a shortcode to display the data on a page with only about 30 seconds of human effort. When I got to my destination, I opened ChatGPT on my dev machine, fed it the new prompt, copied the code, pasted it into my WP backend, performed a code review and security analysis - all passed - and gave it a go. FLAWLESS EXECUTION! Bottom Line: It’s certainly not perfect, and can even create a useless mess of fancy-looking code if you’re not careful, but used right - and in the right circumstances - ChatGPT has cut down on my need for junior dev support significantly, and is especially helpful when the work is outside of my primary programming language. (Getting even a “close enough” framework built for me in a language I'm less familiar with is usually enough for me to be able to take it from there, because programming is programming, regardless of syntax differences.) ChatGPT can build from white-space way faster than I ever could, especially when I don't write in that language everyday. ChatGPT has helped take me go from being a one-or-two language guy to being able to write in almost anything, because it gets me started without much effort. So no, it's not likely replacing me as a “Sr. Dev” anytime soon, but I have replaced about 80% of my reach-outs to Jr's in other languages with ChatGPT alone. Imagine what this thing’s going to be capable of in a few years. GPT-4 is coming next (maybe this?) week, so they say, and I anticipate even bigger improvements in code generation and better handling of more complex prompts, etc. ChatGPT is no joke. As a programmer, you just have to learn how to best leverage it, and know when to put it aside, or to just start over. It won't “take your job” but it might just make you a lot less reliant on others.

question_title: (2) Will ChatGPT replace programmers? - Quora
answer_text: AI won’t replace high-end programmers for while, but I think could seriously break into the more mundane, daily stuff. Here’ my thinking. First there were hard coded programs. Very quickly, memory resident programs replaced instructions on circuit boards. Then came assembly, the ability to create binary code without having to convert each instruction to a binary number. To that point (and this is super condensed), the basic premise of providing the program to the computer remained consistent, just the methodology changed. But then came macro assemblers. Now, instead of just mnemonics that represented instructions, you could instruct your assembler to incorporate pre-written snippets that already had functions coded. Soon, you could reference libraries of common functions, and create and save your own. And with that was born patchwork programming. You still needed a programmer, but what was lost in efficiency of a totally hand-build application was made up for multiple times over in the ability to create new applications in shorter timeframes. Building on that, modern programming languages began to emerge. As those progressed, programs could be built with little reference to binary digits at all. Modern C++ compilers can be instructed to include all kinds of headers and libraries, and the programmer need only make a few declarations, then call those functions without any regard whatsoever as to how they work. AI has progressed to at least the point where it can build a program by essentially pasting bits of code from a vast cache of available sources. It can also interpret human language so as to “understand” the desired outcome of producing code. It’s way faster (no comparison) at searching libraries for the best and most efficient code for any given purpose. Something that takes me 10 minutes to locate by scouring the Internet for examples and open source offerings could be found in milliseconds by an AI module. As this has progressed, AI could now probably replace at least some programmers. And as time passes, that’s likely to become true for more and more levels of programming, even those requiring actual creativity. And I don’t think that’s a good thing in the long run, but that’s another topic.

question_title: (2) Will ChatGPT replace programmers? - Quora
answer_text: Suppose you have an assignment on the Big Bang Theory. In the analogy of a library, we can go into Google and ask it to list a few books on the Big Bang Theory, and it displays you 120 books. What you can do with Chat GPT is ask it to write an essay of 1000 words on the BB Theory derived from these books, and it can do that in 10 seconds. Do you desire that in Shakespearean style? Sure, here it is. What a nice guy! But is this an advantage or a danger? How do we benefit from this? Is it threatening? If so, to whom? What is the actual concern? From the library analogy, we can agree on what the issue is here. This kind of brain power can eliminate creative thought at a frightening magnitude. You will not have to think; just do and follow. But why is that? The root of the problem starts with the school system. Why would you ever cheat on an exam or a paper? That's because the school system values grades more than students value education and learning. So you find other ways for schools to think highly of you. The value we place on a grade is disproportionate to who you are and will become later in life. And at the end of your education, you get a degree because you fooled the system, but did you fool yourself? No, you did not; life will hit hard. And if the chatbot makes people think you are smart even though you are not, who benefits from that? Well, that won't stop its furious propagation. It is a helpful tool if you can't otherwise get something done as well as you could, not a replacement for your own learning. Be flexible with your ambitions, considering the possibility that you might be replaced. All this said, I believe we are still discussing problems of the future here. The current AI will not replace you. What it is doing is extracting a model of the world from the entire corpus of language. It doesn't test its linguistic knowledge against the real world. That's what humans do: come up with a theory and throw it against the world to see if it sticks. AI has a definition of your world—the best way you know how to simplify it into readable and tangible information. Take Van Gogh's "Starry Night." Can AI take this information and develop something equally impressive? Easily. But what AI cannot do is create something so unique that all we can do is draw inspiration from it, as Van Gogh did when he painted the Starry Night. The point is that AI does not have data on events that have not yet occurred. It is keeping up with us, not the other way around. We can be impressed with what AI is doing, and we should be.

answer_text: Extremely unlikely. ChatGPT and similar tools might well get to the point that they can replace things like commercial websites with baskets and payment systems and the like. But we already have those that just need ‘some configuring.’ Replacing the less standard software is likely to be as difficult as ever. Forget the technology for the moment. We have a “hand written” definition of a problem. By some mechanism - whether programmer or ChatGPT - we transform that into something that looks like a solution. But it will contain errors: the specification may be ambiguous, or it may be unambiguous but not what was intended. How are you going to spot that? So a huge part of the effort in developing the system is not in the ‘coding’. It is in the testing and reviewing against the requirement. And there is also a big cost of fixing the system afterwards once a problem has been uncovered. Even the best of all imaginable ChatGPTs is going to fail if the requirement you said is not quite what you meant. ChatGPT and similar tools may change the proportions of time spent on coding, testing and reviewing. But the most costly errors are that affect the customer. The cost is not only the direct part, but any loss of reputation of your company and its products. You risk those at your peril, because bankruptcy may await you if things go badly enough. So the key to a ChatGPT being successful will be if end users encounter less errors, and those that they do as less impactful. I might be wrong, of course, but I do not see how that is achieved.

answer_text: I actually strongly believe that ChatGPT will replace programmers, and it already has. Just this week, I lost my job, which I’d had for almost 3 years. Coincidence? Why are most tech companies laying off now? Why just after the release of ChatGPT? Just this last week, Google layed off over 11,000 employees, its biggest layoff yet. — at the same time as they announced their competitor to Microsoft’s ChatGPT. You can chalk all that down to “pandemic” hiring, but a lot of people who deny this claim, I believe, haven’t used ChatGPT to its fullest. I have — but not as a programmer. I’ve used ChatGPT extensively as a writer over the past 2 weeks to help me write my upcoming LitRPG novel. ChatGPT not only now fully understands the virtual world I’ve created, but it understands the game mechanics better than I ever can. It can build in continuity between my characters, and even points out when my story doesn’t make sense. ChatGPT even writes for me, based on my writing style; when provided the correct prompts, and the correct previous conversation, ChatGPT truly outpaces me as a writer. For programming, ChatGPT can offer some decent (mostly working) starting points, but the code is not great. It requires coaching, but if you provide the source code, their paths, the files, and the technologies used, ChatGPT will almost always do a better job than any junior developer. Senior-level? No. Junior probably — intermediate at best. Ask ChatGPT to generate CSS, and it uses pixels. Any senior front-end developer only sparingly uses pixels and will use rem. But that’s when you ask ChatGPT to use rem — or, better yet, pass it an existing stylesheet from your favourite senior front-end developer that uses rem, and voila. But without the context and the full understanding, ChatGPT probably won’t do the best job. And most people use ChatGPT without providing the full source code, or even accurately describing the problem. The problem isn’t that ChatGPT isn’t smart enough to replace programmers; the problem is that most programmers and non-programmers are not smart enough to use ChatGPT to its fullest. So will ChatGPT replace programmers? Yes, and it already has. Once more tooling becomes mainstream, aside from the obvious GitHub CoPilot, AI will take off and replace a lot of those junior developers, making programming a niche, specialist job like underwater welding. Expect to see this happen in the next 5 years, if not the next 3 years.

I’ve read about what recent developments in AI have been able to achieve with respect to generating code, and while it’s impressive in the sense that I don’t think the AI of 30 years ago could’ve done it, from the perspective of replacing programmers, it’s really not impressive. Like others are saying here, it’s up to the level of a beginning programmer. The more realistic descriptions of these systems are that they could be incorporated into IDEs in the future, to be at the ready to generate needed routines inside of larger software systems; a programmer’s aide, but that’s it. What we’re seeing with AI now is that it’s able to synthesize what we could call “original content” (it’s not just a copy of what someone else wrote), but it doesn’t demonstrate what we would call “thought.” It just has a certain amount of “correctness.” (Incidentally, I think our bureaucratized education system should listen to this distinction closely.) I think what some of the other answers discuss re. ChatGPT is that it’s not able to reliably take multiple valid considerations with code into account. As has been pointed out, it wasn’t designed to be a code generation engine, but a “responder” in conversation. Its “expertise,” if you will, is generating a bunch of sentences that are grammatically correct, and are somehow on the subject that is requested. If one looks at a programming language from this context, you can see how it could generate code, because that’s just another language on which it can analyze and exercise its machine learning techniques. What it produces is syntactically correct, and works semantically, as far as a compiler/interpreter is concerned, but there’s no guarantee, still, that it actually does what you want. It doesn’t mean that what it generates makes logical sense, nor that it takes into account the potential consequences of what it generates. Both of these qualities are very important for being a software engineer. As one of the other answers said, none of this means that people won’t try to use it for creating software. I’m not sure if this is actually happening, but I’ve gotten indications already that there are programmers out there who have been tasked with debugging lots of code generated via. ChatGPT for some project… I hate saying it, but a possible future for programmers is not being replaced by something like this, but being the “cleanup crew” for it. The reason I say this is we’ve seen for a while that most programmers don’t get to work on greenfield projects, but instead, work on pre-existing code, written by other people. It’s conceivable some executives will say, “How about we substitute this AI for ‘other people’, just to get things going?”, because a very common mentality inside of tech firms for decades has been, “Generating code is progress toward getting it done.” That has truth to it, but it’s not the only consideration for a well-functioning system.

question_title: (2) Will ChatGPT replace programmers? - Quora
answer_text: See my answer to the related question: Benjamin Marty · 8y How long until computer programmers will no longer be needed? I graduated from college in 1996, and even those 21+ years ago one professor who taught our programming courses told us about students’ concerns that programmers would no longer be needed at some point during their career. So we have been waiting for this automation for decades, and it doesn’t appear to be coming nearly as fast as some people feared. The professor’s answer at the time, however, was that programmers are really just problem solvers, which will always be needed. Programming has become much more accessible over the past 20 years, and we have more people finding meaningful ways to participate rather than fewer. As a programmer myself, I recently changed projects to start working on a project using a language where you can write 10 to 40 times less code to accomplish complex tasks that used to be much more error prone due to the amount of manually maintained code. So change is already and continuously occurring. Some possibly more relevant questions might be: 1. How long until 90%+ of what programmers spend their time on today is automated? 2. On what will programmers be spending their time when 90%+ of what they used to do is automated? It’s similar to how computer speed and memory capacity changes also changed the problems and applications we deal with. 40 years ago, people didn’t even think about problems or programs that required more than a 1 megabyte of memory to solve, or more than a few billion cycles of processing. So back then, you might not have thought that a 1 MB of memory (let alone 1 GB of memory) would have been necessary for typical computing, or that a 1 MHz processor (let alone 1 GHz) would be useful. Now that we have the technology, we apply it to all sorts of problems and applications we could barely have imagined then. Programmers used to spend a lot of time debugging memory leaks, dealing with fatal application errors, and analyzing code that was unfamiliar or hard to understand. Now those have become much more manageable problems with improved programming languages (with managed-memory), sophisticated debugging software and Intellisense. I probably spent half my time in my first job paging through a programming reference manual. Now I spend only a small fraction of that time looking at documentation because of Intellisense. So likewise, when 90%+ of what programmers spend their time on today is automated, programmers will be free to apply themselves to higher level tasks. They may branch out becoming software architects, designers, business analysts and teachers leaving many of the trivialities of coding behind. And when I talk about teachers, I’m referring to someone who would teach an AI. So I doubt there will be any abrupt point where you can suddenly say that programmers are no longer necessary. Instead programmers will gradually evolve into working differently, and at some point, if you compare what they’re doing to what they do today, they will not look similar any more. But pursuing a career in programming today is likely to be a wise choice even if programming looks very different in 20 years… it’s how you start participating in the evolution. I don’t think computer programmers will be replaced so much as transformed. Tools like ChatGPT have already helped me in my job, and I think I will be able to do new and better things, and have more fun doing them, with tools like ChatGPT. Something better than ChatGPT may transform the profession beyond recognition to the point where programmers and most other professions are being done mostly by AI, but are still being guided by people. Seeing as how that level of technology is pretty close to the technological singularity, it’s hard to predict the kinds of changes we’ll see around that time. I expect such specific questions become almost meaningless at that point compared to the larger context of what kinds of changes are taking place in the economy and society. But for further discussions on those topics, I would refer to Ray Kurzweil and other futurists.

answer_text: As a whole? No. In part? A version of it _might_ down the line reduce part of the load on a set of programmers, and in that way replace _some_ programmers in total. My reasoning It doesn’t understand neither code, nor the social context in which it lives. It has no consideration of context or systems as a whole. It has no sense of management of complexity. It’s neither reliable, nor even consistent. I am aware of how it has been used to scaffold e.g. the core functionality of a browser based snake implementation which immediately looks impressive. Well and nice. Now try to get it to create a complete product. With the entire user flow. Error handling. Performance considerations. Correctness guarantees. Transitions between scenes. The “prompt”(s) appears to me in case to have to be so extensive, detailed and rigorous that it will close to a regular programming language, and thus we’re back to needing people that fluent in those requirements that we once again have programmers. What it will do, however, is allow more people to prototype their ideas, and perhaps get some snippets to get them started when stuck. Which is great. It will probably overlap with a lot of the same cases where no-code solutions also does okay. Apart from that, it’s a very expensive, stochastic rubber duck. But once a system reaches a certain level of complexity or product-readiness - it will still require developers to tie it together. I expect there to be an increased need for developers, not reduced. There will be more ideas put into existence, and more developers will be free to assist on the more mature ideas as they progress. answer_text: Quite a few of the answers are basically saying it doesn’t work well enough to replace programmers. I’m going to go quite a bit further though: even if it worked better, it still wouldn’t replace programmers. What it’s doing is fundamentally different from what programmers do in general. ChatGPT is imitative, not creative. Its imitations are pretty sophisticated, so it can often adapt to the situation at hand pretty well, but what it’s doing is still fundamentally taking things that have been done before, looking at where and how they varied with respect to the situation, and imitating that variation. So, if you ask ChatGPT to help you write code for a homework problem that’s a variation of one of the standard homework questions that’s been around for decades, and people have discussed to death many times over, chances are pretty good that ChatGPT can do quite a good job. Most of programming is about architecture—deciding at a very high level how to take a big complex problem, and break it down into smaller, more manageable pieces. Once you’ve gotten to the level of specific details where ChatGPT can help out noticeably, you’re already dealing with the sorts of things that you’d routinely leave for quite junior programmers anyway. And at least in my experience, even at that level, ChatGPT isn’t nearly as reliable as even the most junior of programmers.

question_title: (2) What are the limitations of ChatGPT? - Quora
answer_text: It is so new that it took time for the first limitations to be noticed. OpenAI’s ChatGPT had its public debut in November, followed by Chat GPT-4 in March, meant to be more powerful. But new research this week reveals a fundamental challenge of developing artificial intelligence: ChatGPT has become worse at performing certain basic math operations. The researchers at Stanford and the University of California, Berkeley, said the deterioration is an example of a phenomenon known to AI developers as drift, where attempts to improve one part of the enormously complex AI models make other parts of the models perform worse. What is a 'AI drift' and why is it making ChatGPT dumber? You may want to rethink using GPT-4, especially for math problems. https://www.zdnet.com/article/what-is-a-ai-drift-and-why-is-it-making-chatgpt-dumber/ Why ChatGPT Is Getting Dumber at Basic Math AI chatbots have stoked fears that they could spin out of control, but they also suffer from a type of deterioration called ‘drift’ https://www.livemint.com/ai/why-chatgpt-is-getting-dumber-at-basic-math-11691172247650.html “Changing it in one direction can worsen it in other directions,” said James Zou, a Stanford professor who’s affiliated with the university’s AI lab and is one of the authors of the research. “It makes it very challenging to consistently improve.” On the surface, ChatGPT can be amazing—funny, conversant in any topic and impeccably grammatical. Some people have given ChatGPT standardized tests that it nailed. But other times the chatbot will flub even basic mathematics. The goal of the researchers, consisting of Lingjiao Chen, a Stanford computer science Ph.D. student, along with Zou and Berkeley’s Matei Zaharia, is to systematically and repeatedly see how models perform over time at a range of tasks. Thus far, they have tested two versions of ChatGPT: version 3.5, available free online, and version 4.0, a premium subscription. The results aren’t entirely promising. They gave the chatbot a basic task: identify whether a particular number is a prime number. This is the sort of math problem that’s complicated for people but simple for computers. To track performance, the researchers fed ChatGPT 1,000 different numbers. In March, the premium GPT-4 correctly identified whether 84% of the numbers were prime or not. (Pretty mediocre performance for a computer, frankly.) By June its success rate dropped to 51%. Across eight different tasks, GPT-4 became worse at six of them. GPT-3.5 improved on six measures but remained worse than its advanced sibling at most of the tasks. Many people who played around with the models were initially dazzled, but over time have started noticing more and more incorrect answers or refusals of the chatbot to respond. The Stanford-Berkeley research shows that it isn’t just anecdotal. The bot has become empirically worse at certain functions, including calculating math questions, answering medical questions and generating code.

Proportional–integral–derivative controller - Wikipedia Control loop feedback mechanism A proportional–integral–derivative controller ( PID controller or three-term controller ) is a feedback -based control loop mechanism commonly used to manage machines and processes that require continuous control and automatic adjustment. It is typically used in industrial control systems and various other applications where constant control through modulation is necessary without human intervention. The PID controller automatically compares the desired target value ( setpoint or SP) with the actual value of the system ( process variable or PV). The difference between these two values is called the error value , denoted as e ( t ) {\displaystyle e(t)} . It then applies corrective actions automatically to bring the PV to the same value as the SP using three methods: The proportional ( P ) component responds to the current error value by producing an output that is directly proportional to the magnitude of the error. This provides immediate correction based on how far the system is from the desired setpoint. The integral ( I ) component, in turn, considers the cumulative sum of past errors to address any residual steady-state errors that persist over time, eliminating lingering discrepancies. Lastly, the derivative ( D ) component predicts future error by assessing the rate of change of the error, which helps to mitigate overshoot and enhance system stability, particularly when the system undergoes rapid changes. The PID output signal can directly control actuators through voltage, current, or other modulation methods, depending on the application. The PID controller reduces the likelihood of human error and improves automation . A common example is a vehicle’s cruise control system . For instance, when a vehicle encounters a hill, its speed will decrease if the engine power output is kept constant. The PID controller adjusts the engine's power output to restore the vehicle to its desired speed, doing so efficiently with minimal delay and overshoot. The theoretical foundation of PID controllers dates back to the early 1920s with the development of automatic steering systems for ships. This concept was later adopted for automatic process control in manufacturing, first appearing in pneumatic actuators and evolving into electronic controllers. PID controllers are widely used in numerous applications requiring accurate, stable, and optimized automatic control , such as temperature regulation , motor speed control, and industrial process management. question_title: (2) What are the advantages of artificial intelligence? - Quora
answer_text: If you mean in what areas is artificial intelligence superior to natural intelligence, the list is so long that we can’t discuss every single aspect here no matter how hard we try. Before we go any further and try to figure out in which way having a brain made out of ones and zeros better than a real brain, we have to understand what exactly is AI because a lot of people tend to misuse the term. There’s a lot of talk about whether the current level of artificial intelligence is capable of real reasoning or “consciousness”. But the truth is that we are as far away from it as we were a couple of decades back. Well, maybe not entirely since I’m not really a scientist and can’t tell you the limits of the current cutting edge technology, but the reason I’m saying this is because most AI nowadays is limited to large language models or LLMs, as I mentioned previously. LLM are basically a black box that ingests HUGE amounts of data and uses machine learning algorithms to predict the most likely text output based on the given input. So the machine is not actually thinking, but instead, simply trying to gauge the most likely sequence of words and letters by learning on the data it’s been given. With that out of the way, here comes the main question: what is this output generating machine actually good at? Well, it can be good at a lot of different things, and it’s getting better and better each and every day, so this post might be outdated in a couple of months time lol. Currently, there’s a lot of buzz around the creative capabilities of AI, as this is the effect people are most likely to pay attention to. Creativity is seen as an inherently human phenomenon, so seeing an algorithm do a better job at creating art or composing music that most people do is very scary for most. This, however, is not even close to being the best use case for something as powerful as what LLMs have: the ability to analyze large amounts of data with reasoning and context awareness. That’s a part of how it because so ubiquitous in the industries requiring precision and high-degree of understanding of very niche topics. Like Finance, for example. As someone who is interested in this field and is aware of most of what’s going on in the industry, I can tell you that I’ve never seen a technology being implemented so rapidly and integrated so deeply into the system. Nothing in finance is done without AI anymore, because it simply does a much better job when given the exact tasks people (yes, traders are people as well, albeit a weird bunch) are absolutely terrible at. That’s why we have seen such a sprawl of trading bots and High Frequency algorithm taking over the majority of trading. As a retail trader, this hits very hard and makes me quite worried about my ability to compete with these ever-evolving algorithms. Seriously, before we had to out analyze other traders to get an edge, but now we have to trade against thousands of algorithms all doing different things and competing against each other and us, although to a lesser extent, included. The only reasonable solution to this issue that I found so far is implementing these AI powered features into my workflow. There is still not a lot of options to choose from, as the retail industry is not very good at keeping up with what the big institutional players are doing. For anyone who’s interested, I found a couple of trading journals with AI statistics that were too immature to use in practice. Like Trader Sync, for example, their AI analysis is not much different from their normal trading stats. I also tried some bots that supposedly make investment decisions based on AI, but ended up simply using chatgpt to make random guesses. Suffice to say, it is not easy to find good trading tools with AI augmentation. Octa is, perhaps, one of the few platforms currently offering native AI support for charting and trade analysis. And even there, the features are still being in active development. Up to this point, I tried the trade analysis tool, which tells me which mistakes I made, what I did correctly, and gives some suggestions for improvement. This one only works on a trade-by-trade basis right now, so I’m still analyzing the overall performance of my account by myself. I hope they’re going to make it, so I don’t have to do that in the future, we’ll see how it goes. There is price pattern detection for certain assets, so I gave it a go as well. Overall, I’d say it’s more of an assistance-focused tool than a signal provider, which is actually a big plus for me personally. Do your own due diligence is something I as a trader take very seriously, and I won’t trust anybody else with doing my analysis. Only helping. I’m not sure how exactly these features will be implemented, but they also promise to add tools for real-time news analysis and additional charting software that is supposed to be better than the current one, I guess. News analysis is actually a big one which I’m hoping will turn out well, because that’s a part that I’m awful at. The current state of news is too chaotic and fast-paced, I don’t how a human being can keep up with everything that’s going on in every part of the world… so I’m definitely going to be delegating this part of my trading routine to AI as soon as possible. That’s my perspective on artificial intelligence, which I hope is quite unique. It will definitely be interesting to see where this goes from now on. The only thing I hope for is that AI is not going to make me obsolete 🥲

answer_text: No, AI won’t reduce jobs. The fears that artificial intelligence will take away jobs are exaggerated. Yes, AI will raise the bar for entrylevel positions, but AI will mostly work as a productivity tool for humans and rather create millions of new jobs. Data being the raw material for AI, most of the jobs will evolve around managing it. The biggest tech buzz in town and AI’s most popular avatar, ChatGPT, can ‘think’ and people are going gaga over its ‘intelligence’. In fact, no other AI tool has generated as much excitement as ChatGPT, launched by San Francisco-based OpenAI, an AI-research lab founded by entrepreneurs Sam Altman, Elon Musk, and others. ChatGPT can compose business e-mails, write creative fiction and code, answer queries, and do more, much to the amazement of its more than one million users worldwide. So, if ChatGPT and other AI platforms can perform tasks that people do, what will humans do. For sure, AI will lower the entry barrier for non-professionals in fields such as coding and content writing. But it will also raise the ceiling for skilled professionals. Humans behind AI - Data being the raw material for AI, most of the jobs will evolve around managing it. For starters, there will be demand for data labelling professionals. For example, an insurance company wants to build a fraud-detection platform to see whether claims are genuine. It has historical data on transactions that are ‘fraud’ and ‘not fraud’. Humans will label this data in either of these categories, feed it to the algorithm, and create the fraud- detection platform. Data annotation will be another big task. For example, in autonomous driving, the car cameras capture images in real time and take immediate decisions. Companies need to annotate the entire data and label accordingly, such as a man crossing a street, or a lamppost. That annotated data is fed into the learning algorithm. Thus, a larger industry around data labelling and annotation will emerge. Humans will also create models for AI to work on. Let’s say a customer relationship management (CRM) platform generates a lot of leads on customers who might be seeking loans from a bank. Some of these leads will get converted while others won’t. Who’s going to build that recommendation algorithm? Many companies will have to create their own models to meet their unique requirements, creating demand for data-science experts who can develop those models. Companies will hire prompt experts as well. These are professionals who develop the prompts or queries for models to produce answers. Each model behaves differently, depending on the prompt. All these roles for labelling, annotations, prompts, and creating models are played by humans and, therefore, these jobs will increase. Moreover, platforms like ChatGPT can’t actually give the right answers without human help. They work on RLHF (reinforcement learning with human feedback), which fine-tunes the choices or answers. So, if there are four answers to a query, the human-trained RLHF that goes into improving the preference model will pick the best answer. As a result, AI platforms will actually improve outcomes for professionals and assist them, rather than replace them. More people will benefit from AI and more ... In these areas AI is mostly helping people be more efficient and meet the extreme levels of demand. Yes, in areas where there is sufficient or excess supply of labour, the answer is yes - these jobs are less needed, and will either be redundant or evolve in their nature But it’s in the ‘long term’ where things get really interesting. There’s no consensus on whether and when we’ll get something like true Artificial General Intelligence, but many people (and I’m one of them) believe that we will. AGI will completely transform the future of work. Even with narrow AI, we’re now seeing AI having impact in areas that were previously thought ‘off limits’ - for example in pure maths and theoretical physics.
