answer_text: The number of "vibe coding will replace programmers" posts, has officially become annoying. So it's time to bring in the heavy hitters in formal computational theory, which none of the vibe coders actually studied. Rice-Shapiro is a constellation of formal mathematical proofs, about programs that write and analyze other programs. Those proofs affect every vibe-coding startup you are in love with right now. Among other incredibly important things, these theorems state that it is IMPOSSIBLE to implement an AI, that can even CHECK whether an arbitrary program is "correct"... for whatever definition of correct you can reasonably imagine. Note that I didn't say "it would be really hard." I also didn't say "I can't imagine that". I said IMPOSSIBLE, and I meant it, and so did Henry Gordon Rice, when he put it into his doctoral dissertation. Rice-Shapiro, along with its ancillary proofs, puts hard limits on how accurate AI analysis of software can EVER be. Rice-Shapiro and friends are PROOFS. These are not "the CEO of this AI company thinks" or "some rando social media thought leader predicts" or “I saw on X today that”. These proofs will NEVER be outdone by a younger and sexier proof. These proofs will be valid, and they will continue to be correct, a thousand years from now. No, your fancy AI will not replace programmers. Your AI can't even tell you what an arbitrary program DOES, much less whether it is correct. And these facts, you can bank on for the next thousand years or ten thousand, as fits your fancy.

As it stands, you need someone who knows what they’re doing to find and root out those bugs. And even getting past the issue of bugs, there’s a further problem with LLMs which is that they often produce sprawling and inefficient code. LLMs will often right lengthy scripts to solve problems that could be fixed in a couple of lines. This makes them inefficient, harder to understand and harder to debug. answer_text: Anyone who says so either doesn’t write code for a living or is trying to sell you something. Either way, they don’t know what they are talking about. How can vibe coding be the future? The people who are pushing this as “You prompt and let AI do the hard work for you!” don’t explain how this works when it comes to making usable, maintainable software. For the simple fact that most of the people push this can’t read code! You know what I tell people I teach in writing software? You have to learn to read code before you can write it. If I point to a snippet of code, I ask them what it will do when run. If they respond with “Uhhh…”, how can you write code? You have to know what to write first and have a sense of what it is going to do beforehand. Learning to read code first is mandatory. Ever notice we learn to read before we learn to write as children? Because we have to know what the symbols mean, how to use them and so on before we can assemble them on our own. Code is just specialized language and you think in it like any other. Vibe coding is just another pitch that the low/no-skilled person can use an AI assistant to do the “hard” part of writing code. The human takes the code, and if it compiles and runs, sees a result they are expecting. Or looks right. If they can’t read the code, their own anthropomorphic biases are going to kick in and tell them that it does. AI is smarter than people, AI knows what is doing, AI knew what I wanted. It looks right therefore it is right. Until it isn’t. Then the whole edifice comes crashing down because code does not exist in a vacuum. It exists for purpose. Those who want the solution are going to notice if it is not working. Often because their own futures might depend on it so they will use more traditional means to check the work if problems get reported. And then the vibe coder will be forced to explain what is wrong against demands to fix it. I want to see what a debugging session on previously generated code looks like. Vibe debugging is going to be a lot more interesting than vibe coding because there is no LLM for that thought process and troubleshooting errant code the generator understands nothing about conceptually! AI is pattern matching on stuff it has seen before. It is not reasoning. It cannot deduce a solution from a description of a problem. It is vomiting out someone else’s solution and playing “fill in the blanks” for the rest. You have no idea if the values it is plugging in are valid for need. The person vibe coding will get a tingle and think they’re being productive not realizing that feeling is not the sign of something good coming. Do you know how many times I’ve heard people talk about the future of software development in my career? Do you know what the ditches of the Information Superhighway are littered with? The wreckage and debris of failures that were “The Next Big Thing”. This trend is going to be short and painful. Like a runaway truck hitting a VW Golf. Vibe coding is useful for people who can already read and write code. Then it acts as an overgrown “type ahead” and active Stack Overflow hint provider. Not a solution builder. I’ve long said you can’t Google your way to success in software engineering and doing it in natural language with a silicon parrot does not change the outcome.

question_title: (2) Will OpenAI GPT 5 be able to surpass upper average computer programmers? - Quora
answer_text: If AI could produce guaranteed-to-work, best-practices-compliant maintainable code on first try, && understood and correctly implemented requirements and changes like a human programmer does, && accepted responsibility and wrote software accordingly, && had a general and updated awareness of what is happening in the real world (business SWOT etc.), && knew how to get unstuck if something wrong? Then yes. Otherwise, no. I am betting on no. The reasons being: Given what I’ve seen so far from all AI models, there’s a 90% chance the code produced on first try does not work. Giving information wrt to requirements can be misunderstood and introducing changes confuses AI. The more changes you ask it to implement, the worse the code becomes. AI cannot assume legal responsibility—because it’s a non-living entity. If it makes decisions that are statistically ‘correct’, there’s a high chance something could go wrong because the real world is full of gotchas (NNT calls this the ‘sucker problem’ due to how things happen in ‘Extremistan’) and statistical prediction works only in Normalistan (to continue coining a similar term)—it being a small subset of the real world. question_title: (2) Will OpenAI GPT 5 be able to surpass upper average computer programmers? - Quora
answer_text: Given it doesn’t exist yet, we can only wildly speculate… Though there are suggestions that LLMs can only go so far before reaching fundamental capability limits — kind of the way a bicycle can only carry loads so heavy, and so far, and so fast, before you have to change technology to carry more farther and faster. But more importantly, it doesn’t matter if some future — or current — LLM can emit better code faster than an “upper average” computer programmer, because just being a code generator is not what being a computer programmer or software engineer is about. It’s about being able to design effective solutions to business problems that are poorly specified, sometimes outright wrong or politically tinged, and that require deep knowledge of current project source code, other projects, in-house and external APIs, in-house and external and often proprietary libraries, services, databases, enormous database schemas, policies, procedures, processes, documentation, documents, legislation, rules, and laws. Many — and sometimes all — of those are fundamental to virtually every enterprise software engineering task. The sort of simple, standalone, scholastic-type programming problems so easily written by ChatGPT are nothing like most real enterprise programming requirements. But the biggest limitation is that it’s simply utterly unreasonable to enter and repeatedly re-enter source code, schemas, business rules, you-name-it, for every new programming problem. Not to mention the fact that expressing requirements in natural language is one of the worst ways to specify solutions. It’s verbose, ambiguous, unclear, and arduously slow. That’s because software engineers think in code. The easiest and fastest way for them to express solutions is to write the code to implement them. Forcing developers to chat their requirements in English is like asking a native French speaker to write a French essay by translating what he wants to write into English, writing the rules and conditions of the essay in English, and then passing the lot to a mediocre translation service to translate the English into French, and then have the native French speaker edit it. Terrible. That said, I have no doubt future editions of ChatGPT — or its successors or competitors — will become useful tools for programmers, just as compilers, libraries, frameworks, code generators, IDEs, debuggers, and so forth have done in the past. But except for some limited uses, mainly around learning unfamiliar languages or APIs, they’re not there yet.

answer_text: I can’t answer specifically about OpenAI models; most of my experience has been with Anthropic and Claude tools, which I think are very good, if used properly. So I’m going to answer more generally, and hopefully that addresses some of what you’re asking. (1) These tools already are faster at code generation than a human, of course. (2) When you combine the generation time with the cycling to fix errors and get things running, and the time taken to prompt and guide the tools, surprisingly enough there isn’t as much efficiency as you think. There is a good recent study which is generating a lot of discussion: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity We conduct a randomized controlled trial to understand how early-2025 AI tools affect the productivity of experienced open-source developers working on their own repositories. Surprisingly, we find that when developers use AI tools, they take 19% longer than without—AI makes them slower. https://metr.org/blog/2025-07-10-early-2025-ai-experienced-os-dev-study/ (3) The tools are great at generating code from prompt descriptions, and TERRIBLE at generating strong tests. There is a very strong tendency to generate vacuous tests that pass, especially when the tool sits in a loop — it might generate a pretty good test as a first pass, which fails, and then Claude Code tends to weaken the test, rather than strengthening the code. So much so, that my guidelines for myself and my team is that AI cannot write the test, humans do, but AI can write code until it passes the tests, without weakening them. This is a crucial thing, more below. (4) The tools are predictably bad about respecting API contracts or other external constraints — mainly this is because the tool can’t really tell that certain things should not be touched from just looking at the code or your prompt itself. Left to its own devices, the model will happily optimize away arguments in functions, which is fine for private methods, but what if the function is an API handler? You’ve just broken the interface with customers who are writing their own code and consider the API a contract! This is crucial and VERY HARD thing to fix, more below. Basically, these models already surpass the speed of a human programmer (any!) on raw code generation. But raw code generation is a small part of the task of programming. If the question is “when will AI models be able to completely replace a human programmer”, then the answer will involve AI models having the ability to gain the kind of domain knowledge and context that the human programmer has, and then the ability to reason over that domain knowledge AND the prompt to produce results that are safe and do not break APIs, and that produce “strong” tests, not weak ones. In particular, to do this independently of a human programmer, the model has to be able to reason about negative space — what should you NOT do, what is MISSING from a specification, etc., and there is a good bit of research which shows that this is not just hard for LLMs to do, but architecturally something that “next word predictors” are not suited for. We need additional architecture to do this, not just bigger LLMs. I suspect that we’re more than a model generation away, we’re missing something architectural about thinking and reasoning. But, work on AI is iterating quickly, and we’ll see what happens in the next few years.

question_title: (2) Will OpenAI GPT 5 be able to surpass upper average computer programmers? - Quora
answer_text: In some ways yes, and in others no. GPT 5 and other models will be far better than any programmer at quickly generating large bodies of working code. But they will have three limitations: (1). They will still be prone to egregious errors. Think of the AI generated pictures we’ve all seen that are amazingly good, except for the person who has six fingers. Therefore, AI output will need to be carefully scrutinized and tested. (2). They are not yet good at architecting complete solutions to large problems. There are several reasons for this, and it’s going to be a hard problem to solve. (3). They are not good at inferring requirements. Humans take into account many implicit requirements and goals when writing code. These requirements need to be explicitly stated for the AI. Personally, I think we are approaching the limits of LLMs, and that future progress is going to require a combination of techniques. But that means progress is going to slow down, because we need to experiment and figure things out, rather than just pouring on more data and more processing power.

For example the question explicitly states that you have to rotate a matrix using algorithm that uses at most O something memory and time and return it. This is not the case in other situations, because the questions are very “practical" and “fairy-tale like" and it is your task to actually “convert" that to some theoretical problem. You know, for example, the question is like “Bob wants to put a fence around his oddly shaped garden, how much material does he need?”, and it is up to you to deduce that it is actually some unique case of the Convex hull problem and you need to implement it to get a solution. You often have no specific hint of how fast your algorithm should be (in terms of big O complexity), it is up to you to come up with the solution that will be able to process the inputs in the given time and memory limit. question_title: (2) What is a generative AI? - Quora
answer_text: Generative AI refers to artificial intelligence systems that have the ability to generate content, such as text, images, audio, or video, often in a creative and human-like manner. There are several types of generative AI models and techniques that have been developed. Some of the notable types of generative AI include: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs): GANs consist of two neural networks, a generator and a discriminator, that are trained together in a competitive process. The generator creates data, while the discriminator tries to distinguish between real and generated data. Over time, the generator improves its ability to produce content that is increasingly realistic. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs): RNNs are a type of neural network that is well-suited for sequential data, such as text and time series. They have been used for generating text and music, as well as for language modeling. Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) Networks: LSTMs are a type of RNN that can capture longer-range dependencies in data. They are commonly used in text generation, machine translation, and speech recognition. Transformer Models: Transformer models, such as GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer) and BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers), have made significant advancements in natural language understanding and generation. GPT, for example, is a powerful model for text generation and has been used for applications like language translation and content generation. Variational Autoencoders (VAEs): VAEs are generative models that are often used in image and video generation. They encode input data into a lower-dimensional space and then decode it to generate new data. VAEs are used in applications like image generation and style transfer. Autoencoders: Autoencoders are neural networks used for data compression and reconstruction. Variations of autoencoders, such as denoising autoencoders, can be employed for generative tasks. Reinforcement Learning: Reinforcement learning agents can be trained to generate sequences of actions, making them suitable for tasks like video game playing and robotics. question_title: (2) What is a generative AI? - Quora
answer_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) describes algorithms (such as Chat GPT → Generative Pretrained Transformer ) that can be used to create new content, including audio, code, images, text, simulations, and videos. Recent breakthroughs in the field have the potential to drastically change the way we approach content creation. For Understanding Generative AI first you have to understand AI & ML: Artificial Intelligence is pretty much just what it sounds like—the practice of getting machines to mimic human intelligence to perform tasks. You’ve probably interacted with AI even if you don’t realize it—voice assistants like Siri and Alexa are founded on AI technology, as are customer service chatbots that pop up to help you navigate websites. Machine learning is a type of artificial intelligence. Through machine learning, practitioners develop artificial intelligence through models that can “learn” from data patterns without human direction. The unmanageably huge volume and complexity of data (unmanageable by humans, anyway) that is now being generated has increased machine learning’s potential, as well as the need for it. What does it take to build a Generative AI Model? Building a generative AI model has for the most part been a major undertaking, to the extent that only a few will-resourced tech heavyweights have made an attempt. Open AI, the company behind Chat GPT, former GPT models, and DALL-E, has billions in funding from bold-face-name donors. DeepMind is a subsidiary of Alphabet, the parent company of Google, and even Meta has dipped a toe into the generative AI model pool with its Make-A-Video product. These companies employ some of the world’s best computer scientists and engineers. But it’s not just talent. When you’re asking a model to train using nearly the entire internet, it’s going to cost you. Open AI hasn’t released exact costs, but estimates indicate that GPT-3 was trained on around 45 terabytes of text data—that’s about one million feet of bookshelf space, or a quarter of the entire Library of Congress—at an estimated cost of several million dollars. These aren’t resources your garden-variety start-up can access. What kind of output can a Generative AI model produce? As you may have noticed above, outputs from generative AI models can be indistinguishable from human-generated content, or they can seem a little uncanny. The results depend on the quality of the model—as we’ve seen, Chat GPT’s outputs so far appear superior to those of its predecessors—and the match between the model and the use case, or input. Chat GPT can produce what one commentator called a ”solid A-” essay comparing theories of nationalism from Benedict Anderson and Ernest Gellner—in ten seconds. It also produced an already famous passage describing how to remove a peanut butter sandwich from a VCR in the style of the King James Bible. Image-generating AI models like DALL-E 2 can create strange, beautiful images on demand, like a Raphael painting of Madonna and child, eating pizza. Other generative AI models can produce code, video, audio, or business simulations. But the outputs aren’t always accurate—or appropriate. When Priya Krishna asked DALL-E 2 to come up with an image for Thanksgiving dinner, it produced a scene where the turkey was garnished with whole limes, set next to a bowl of what appeared to be guacamole. For its part, Chat GPT seems to have trouble counting, or solving basic algebra problems—or, indeed, overcoming the sexist and racist bias that lurks in the undercurrents of the internet and society more broadly. Generative AI outputs are carefully calibrated combinations of the data used to train the algorithms. Because the amount of data used to train these algorithms is so incredibly massive—as noted, GPT-3 was trained on 45 terabytes of text data—the models can appear to be “creative” when producing outputs. What’s more, the models usually have random elements, which means they can produce a variety of outputs from one input request—making them seem even more lifelike. What kind of problems can a Generative AI model solve? The opportunity for businesses is clear. Generative AI tools can produce a wide variety of credible writing in seconds, then respond to criticism to make the writing more fit for purpose. This has implications for a wide variety of industries, from IT and software organizations that can benefit from the instantaneous, largely correct code generated by AI models to organizations in need of marketing copy. In short, any organization that needs to produce clear written materials potentially stands to benefit. Organizations can also use generative AI to create more technical materials, such as higher-resolution versions of medical images. And with the time and resources saved here, organizations can pursue new business opportunities and the chance to create more value. We’ve seen that developing a generative AI model is so resource intensive that it is out of the question for all but the biggest and best-resourced companies. Companies looking to put generative AI to work have the option to either use generative AI out of the box or fine-tune them to perform a specific task. If you need to prepare slides according to a specific style, for example, you could ask the model to “learn” how headlines are normally written based on the data in the slides, then feed it slide data and ask it to write appropriate headlines.

answer_text: (For the record, I'm not counting 2023 movies that were released in some areas in 2024 like The Zone of Interest or Poor Things. Also my favourite genre is horror, so there's obviously going to be a bias there). So far 2024 has been fairly average in terms of movies I've enjoyed. I still have a number of titles on my to-watch list (Longlegs, Late Night With The Devil, One Life, Civil War, Apartment 7A, The Exorcism, Megalopolis) so I'll suspend final judgement until I've ticked those off, but for now the list of 2024 movies I've watched and really, really liked is a short one- just 3 titles, in fact: 1.V/H/S/Beyond. I've been a fan of the famed anthology/found footage franchise since the beginning, but it's fair to say that it's had an output over the years that could best be described as uneven. Up till now probably the best entry was V/H/S/94, which was rare in that (wraparound story aside) every segment in it was of pretty much equally excellent quality, with one, The Subject, being arguably the best in the entire franchise. After a couple of overall fairly average sequels in between (though To Hell And Back from V/H/S/99 definitely stood out, as did No Wake/Ambrosia from V/H/S/85), however, the franchise is very much back on top form with Beyond, an entry mostly focusing on the theme of alien abduction (first touched upon in V/H/S/2's Slumber Party segment), which gives 94 itself a run for its money as the best entry in the saga. Pretty much all the entries are decent, with the absolute standouts being Live And Let Dive, in which a birthday skydiving event goes horribly wrong after a few uninvited guests join the party at several thousand feet, and Fur Babies, a grisly and darkly comedic thriller involving an overenthusiastic “dog lady” with a few secrets to hide, written and directed by (but strangely enough not staring) horror icon Justin Long. 2.MaXXXine. I was very much looking forward to the concluding part of Ti West and Mia Goth's X trilogy, and although it isn't the best one in the series (that honour firmly belongs to 2022's Pearl in my opinion) I definitely wasn't disappointed. While X clearly took inspiration from the gritty, scuzzy nastiness of early slasher movies like the original Texas Chain Saw Massacre, and Pearl was an homage not only to the vividly colourful giallos of Mario Bava but also to early Technicolor productions in general like The Wizard of Oz, MaXXXine roots itself firmly in the coke-fuelled sleazy glamour and bloody practical effects of the 1980s video nasties. Following Goth's Maxine Minx as she attempts to leave behind her experiences in X while struggling to make it big in Hollywood set against the real-life backdrop of the infamous Night Stalker murders, MaXXXine boasts a stellar cast, a gripping- if ultimately slightly convoluted and unsatisfying- narrative, oodles of atmosphere and some fantastic practical effects. 3.Deadpool & Wolverine. I've never been much of an MCU fan (even back when it was good), but I've always enjoyed the Deadpool movies, and it was great to finally see the Reynolds-Jackman teamup that's been teased for so long. The plot is pretty meandering and convoluted (I'm aware of the deliberate attempt to critique the laziness of parallel universes in modern superhero fiction, but at what point does the critique become the very thing it's attempting to criticise?) and not being up-to-date on every MCU-related project and piece of news I'm sure a lot of the meta jokes went over my head, but overall D&W was a hell of a fun ride with a lot of laugh-out-loud moments that, for once in a contemporary MCU movie, actually landed. As a movie it's pretty decent if flawed (a bit better than Deadpool 2, but not as good as the first one would be my assessment), but if you go into it purely to experience the Ryan-Hugh bromance and the snarky humour resultant from this (not to mention the near-constant shitting on the MCU as a whole, which is something that will never get old for me), then you definitely won't be disappointed. Honourable mention: The Ministry Of Ungentlemanly Warfare. It's pretty far from Guy Ritchie's best work and frankly didn't leave much of an impression on me, but it was a fun experience while it lasted. Which is more than can be said for a lot of movies this year... In terms of movies yet to be released (where I am at least), I have two that are definitely my most anticipated. The first is Terrifier 3, which is coming to my local cinema on Halloween (especially appropriate given that Art the Clown's feature-length debut was in 2013 anthology All Hallows' Eve). I've followed the franchise with enthusiasm ever since the release of Terrifier 2 two years ago, which I consider to be the best slasher film of this century so far (I didn't care that much for the first Terrifier which was frankly a bit boring and one-dimensional, though I do like the original short film* from 2011 that was eventually repurposed for All Hallow's Eve), and given that the third one is being described almost universally as bigger, better and more extreme then I'm very much looking forward to experiencing it first hand (the trailer looks fantastic). The fact that, as with the second one, people are passing out, throwing up and in some cases not even making it past the first scene of the movie, combined with the fact that it's the first movie to be given the extremely rare “forbidden for those under 18” rating in France since 2006's Saw III (which I've always found ironic given that France is the country that gave us Martyrs, Inside and Gaspar Noé), is the cherry on top. Let's just say that if at least one person in the cinema doesn't puke when I'm watching it (it won't be anyone in my group as I'll be going alone, since I can't find anyone among my friends or family who wants to watch it with me lol), I'll be pretty disappointed. My only worry is that given how much the movie has been built up over the past few weeks, I have no idea how it's going to actually deliver, to meet my expectations. But I have faith in Damien Leone; after all, apparently one scene even made David Howard Thornton, Art the Clown himself, feel a little unwell. My other most anticipated movie of this year is Robert Eggers' Nosferatu remake, coming out this December. I'm a huge fan of Eggers' work so far, and given how much he was clearly influenced by German Expressionism in the cinematography of The Lighthouse (one of my top 5 movies of 2019, a year that saw the release of some of the best films of the decade like Joker, Parasite, 1917 and Once Upon A Time In Hollywood so it was up against some stiff competition) it makes sense for him to tackle the OG German Expressionist movie itself. FW Murnau's seminal vampire classic from 1922 already saw two remakes in the 1970s, both by Werner Herzog (one in English and one in German), so it'll be interesting to see how Eggers' version compares both to those and to Murnau's original. It'll be good to see Bill Skarsgard get his teeth into (pun very much intended) Count Orlok, a horror role that is quite a bit different from Pennywise, and having regular Eggers contributor Willem Dafoe (The Lighthouse, The Northman) playing the Abraham Van Helsing role (named Professor Von Franz in the movie) is a nice touch, given that he played Count Orlok in 2000's Shadow of the Vampire, a fictional reimagining of the making of the original Nosferatu. A24's new horror film Heretic with Hugh Grant also looks pretty good, I'm definitely looking forward to that one. I was also really looking forward to Saw 11 after how surprisingly excellent 2023's Saw X was. It was supposed to be releasing about now, but unfortunately for some reason Lionsgate pushed the release back by a year, so we're going to have to wait till next October for that one. *yes, potential horror pedants reading this, I am aware that the actual first short film to feature Art was 2008's The 9th Circle (also incorporated into All Hallows' Eve).

It’s why I find it odd when I see so many teenagers online claiming to be depressed. It’s possible for anyone, but it can’t be *everyone*. In July, I started going to a library to regain my focus. That’s where I discovered Quora in this new way. Before that, I thought it was just a knowledge-sharing site. Then, just 2-3 days later, I started writing on it, and that was one of the best decisions I made. I hadn’t used Instagram, Snapchat, or WhatsApp for months (WhatsApp only every 4-5 days for updates). I never shared anything online—no DPs, no statuses, no stories. Everything was just happening within me. And honestly, when someone is truly in such a phase, they don’t have the time or energy to show it off. Sharing something with close ones is a different matter. AUR I WISH ALL WITH MY HEART THE SUCCESS TO THE PERSON; NOT MATTER IF SOMEONE HURT ME ALSO, 0 HATE FOR ANYONE :P BUT NO HAPPY, NO HAPPINESS FOR ME :) AUGUST – NOVEMBER I stopped trying—that thing I’d been trying for 3 months. This period was very depressing. I watched 50+ episodes of Crime Patrol and over 50 true crime documentaries and movies—just to distract myself. At one point, my screen time reached 16-17 hours a day. Yes, I wasn’t studying much during this time, but I have no regrets because that phase was real. Also watched 4 movies in theatre this year (Hn akele hi, mazaa aata hai) October came—it was my birthday. I didn’t feel like doing anything, but for my family, I cut a cake. Just two friends were there, and I went to the temple and distributed food (which felt like the best feeling ever). In November, I visited my grandmother’s house again after a year. There was a wedding (a cousin sister’s) followed by another (a cousin brother’s). It was nice meeting relatives (mine don’t taunt me, which is good, and I know how to handle things). DECEMBER Things started to improve. Slowly, I got back to studying. My focus had been gone, but I started taking offline tests. At first, I scored 15%, but now I’ve reached 55%. It was very tough, but I made it. Now, I don’t ask anything from God—not like I used to. My prayers are simple: “May your day be auspicious, and may you grant me good sense.” I don’t blame God for anything because when things were great, it was because of Him too (especially the last 6-7 years, not counting 2024). God has given me a healthy body, parents, and opportunities, so I have to make something of myself. I don’t regret wasting time this year because it was bound to happen. The fact that I came out of it without harming myself—that’s an achievement for me. And till now, I can’t believe what happened. I'M TRYING MY HARD AND I WILL . I CAN AND I WILL I'LL GIVE MY 100% MAA PAPA KO PROUD KARANA HAI, EK BAAR COLLEGE JAAKE APNE PASSION KO ACHE SE CONTINUE KARNA HAI AUR BSS THODI SI, I MEAN ZYADA SE DUNIYA GHUMNI HAI (SOLO TRAVEL), HA BICH- BICH ME WITH MAA PAPA. I’ve written too much again—oh no…. In a while, everyone will go crazy about the new year, but since it’s New Year’s, there’s not much to watch anyway. works out for me- especially for this post. If you’ve made till here then do leave a comment. Honestly, I don’t believe much in the New Year—our real one comes in April. But since this calendar is what we follow, we have to go along with it. So, HAPPY 2025 to all of you! My wishes may not make it happen, but may God make it a great year for you. question_title: (2) How has 2024 been for you? - Quora
answer_text: Hello readers, This time I would start with an honest confession. As I have religiously followed the tradition of writing a blog that summarizes my entire year, this year I thought of skipping it. Reason being, a lot, really, a lot has happened this year, and I wasn't sure whether I would be able to make justice to everything that has happened by writing a single blog post. And a part of me has given up on writing because I felt a lot of things did leave me, so why not let go another hobby. But as I am back home, I was reminded that end of the day, this is where I can always come back to. This applies for 'selfamuser' as well. This is my HOME. I don't know if I'll ever be able to explain verbally the things that I have written, but this is who I am, this is what I hold up to and my blogs are the gateway to myself. So giving up on something that I so dearly love wasn't a wise choice. So here I am, at 23rd December going to journal one of the most iconic year of my life. This year I left home, started off with my MBA, lived in hostel, met a bunch of new characters, became a part of memories that are worth sharing with the grandkids. Sounds fun! Yes it is! Living on your own is definitely fun when you have the right people by your side. Strangely I did meet some of them and life seemed good and happy. But life doesn't feel good everyday. To be honest, I have stopped paying attention to sadness. I have made peace with the fact life will always be trashy. People who love you today will forget your existence the next day, the work that you are appreciated for today, will be thrown upon as a expected burden tomorrow. However you try, you will always end up somewhere shittier, and that's the goddamn beauty of your twenty's. I have had quite a few achievements this year, but I have also terribly failed. I felt belonged amidst the crowd, and I also felt I have no one in this universe. I wanted to leave everything and come back to my mom, as I felt shifting out has been one of the worst decision of my life. But do you know what? I survived everything and not only that I also did thrive in some contexts. And I am glad that I moved out. Things are going to be way more tough, but I love the woman I am becoming. Not rationalising upon how good or bad I have become, all I know is my younger self would be very proud of me. She won't judge me whether I have won or lost, she would just be happy seeing I am doing things, I am trying, may be gradually but I am doing what I promised her I'll do. I know I'll get better at this, and maybe that will suffice for now. Slowly and steadily you learn to do things, you change and grow and all of a sudden you become that adult who fucks up less! Grateful for 2024! Cheers 🥂

Affiliate marketing is an advertising model in which a company compensates third-party publishers to generate traffic or leads to the company’s products and services. The third-party publishers are affiliates, and the commission fee incentivizes them to find ways to promote the company. OR Affiliate marketing is a type of performance-based marketing where individuals or businesses, known as affiliates, earn a commission for promoting another company's products or services. Affiliates typically receive a unique tracking link or code to share with their audience, and when someone makes a purchase through that link, the affiliate earns a percentage of the sale. It's a popular way for companies to expand their reach and for individuals to monetize their online presence. Is there anything specific you'd like to know about affiliate marketing? KEY TAKEAWAYS Affiliate marketing is a marketing scheme in which a company compensates partners for business created from the affiliate's marketing tactics. Digital marketing, analytics, and cookies have made affiliate marketing a billion-dollar industry. Firms typically pay affiliates per sale and less frequently by clicks or impressions. The three main types of affiliate marketing are unattached affiliate marketing, involved affiliate marketing, and related affiliate marketing. Understanding Affiliate Marketing The internet has increased the prominence of affiliate marketing. Amazon (AMZN) popularized the practice by creating an affiliate marketing program whereby websites and bloggers put links to the Amazon page for a reviewed or discussed product to receive advertising fees when a purchase is made. In this sense, affiliate marketing is essentially a pay-for-performance marketing program where the act of selling is outsourced across a vast network. Affiliate marketing predates the Internet, but in the world of digital marketing, analytics, and cookies made it a billion-dollar industry. A company running an affiliate marketing program can track the links that bring in leads and, through internal analytics, see how many convert to sales. An e-commerce merchant wanting to reach a wider base of internet users and shoppers may hire an affiliate. An affiliate could be the owner of multiple websites or email marketing lists; the more websites or email lists that an affiliate has, the wider its network. The hired affiliate then communicates and promotes the products offered on the e-commerce platform to their network. The affiliate does this by running banner ads, text ads, posting links on its websites, or sending emails to clientele. Firms use advertisements in the form of articles, videos, and images to draw an audience’s attention to a service or product. Visitors who click the ads or links are redirected to the e-commerce site. If they purchase the product or service, the e-commerce merchant credits the affiliate’s account with the agreed-upon commission, which could be 5% to 10% of the sales price. Types of Affiliate Marketing There are three main types of affiliate marketing: unattached affiliate marketing, related affiliate marketing, and involved affiliate marketing. Unattached Affiliate Marketing: This is an advertising model in which the affiliate has no connection to the product or service they are promoting. They have no known related skills or expertise and do not serve as an authority on or make claims about its use. This is the most uninvolved form of affiliate marketing. The lack of attachment to the potential customer and product absolves the affiliate from the duty to recommend or advise. Related Affiliate Marketing: As the name suggests, related affiliate marketing involves the promotion of products or services by an affiliate with some type of relationship to the offering. Generally, the connection is between the affiliate's niche and the product or service. The affiliate has enough influence and expertise to generate traffic, and their level of authority makes them a trusted source. The affiliate, however, makes no claims about the use of the product or service. Involved Affiliate Marketing: This type of marketing establishes a deeper connection between the affiliate and the product or service they're promoting. They have used or currently use the product and are confident that their positive experiences can be shared by others. The return on investment for affiliate marketing is high as the company only pays on traffic converted to sales. The cost of advertising, if any, is borne by the affiliate. As technology evolved, the focus turned to commissions on actual sales or qualified leads. The early affiliate marketing programs were vulnerable to fraud because clicks could be generated by software, as could impressions. Now, most affiliate programs have strict terms and conditions on how to generate leads. There are also certain banned methods, such as installing adware or spyware that redirect all search queries for a product to an affiliate's page. Some affiliate marketing programs go as far as to lay out how a product or service is to be discussed in the content before an affiliate link can be validated. So an effective affiliate marketing program requires some forethought. The terms and conditions must be clearly spelled out, especially if the contract agreement pays for traffic rather than sales. The potential for fraud in affiliate marketing is possible. Unscrupulous affiliates can squat on domain names with misspellings and get a commission for the redirect. They can populate online registration forms with fake or stolen information, and they can purchase AdWords on search terms the company already ranks high on, and so on. Even if the terms and conditions are clear, an affiliate marketing program requires that someone monitor affiliates and enforce rules. So, coming to 2023, nah, not this time. I didn’t start with any resolutions. I gave up on them 5 years ago, so thankfully I didn’t spend a penny on a gym subscription in January. I took it on in February for the whole year. Now it has become a different story. However, in February, I had planned a trip to Goa, so I postponed my gym to March even though I had already paid for it. I think I slept for 2–3 hours, and suddenly it was June. I remember August because I broke my rib cage. Oh, the sweet pain and the nightmare of dealing with it. If you think a breakup hurts more, try breaking your bone. Well, I needed recovery, so two more months were gone. Meanwhile, I started working on a novel. A poor guy who was bedridden, who had nothing to do except eating and cursing my fate on fracture recovery. Something had to be done, so I wrote my first chapter, which I published in December. You know when you have nothing to do, either you waste time or you waste time. Procrastination has nothing to do with your planning. And when you are good at something, you don’t need an excuse for it; you just do it, and excuses will come automatically. Perhaps, this is the summary of my whole new year. There are no regrets, and there is no particular achievement to remember. As you grow older, you learn that few things matter. For the things I was crying and cursing about 5 or 10 years ago doesn’t mean anything to me now. So when I say there are some ups and downs, well, those are part of life, and those things give more meaning to your life. I am glad I have made a few memories, and one milestone I achieved is cutting all toxic people from my life. They don’t need me, and more than that, I don’t need them. Sometimes, I feel bad that I lost people from my life, but it is important to acknowledge that they were not healthy for my mental peace. Trust me, it worked like a wonder. Then I slept. answer_text: Probably the most anxiety driven yet wholesome year. I started off the year in the UK. My manifested dream from 2019 to spend Christmas ’22 and NYE ’22–23 in the royal abode. And though it all sounded all fancy and lovely for others to hear, all I felt was sad and alone. Call it seasonal depression contributed by the freezing temperatures or my mind playing games, whether or not I was ready to move to a foreign land leaving my parents behind. A year ago, today - 6th Jan, I also found out that I had failed my PLAB 2 exam by 0.5 marks, in spite of passing the required number of stations. It was heart breaking. More because, I knew how capable and deserving I was. My friends who hadn’t prepared well, and were luxuriously spending thousands of pounds in the UK had passed. I spent my entire trip studying and practising. I didn’t go sight seeing or to grab a bite, devoting my entire time to practising and yet I failed. I had almost given up. My last step towards my dream in the UK- and I had been told that I didn’t make it? How could it be possible? I had been working so hard towards it for the past several months.. Seeing the result, and having no one to talk, to hug, cry to or run for comfort wasn’t easy either. My clinical attachment had just ended and I couldn’t wait to just be back home. It was not just a failure. It was a COSTLY failure. Mid Jan, I was home and I cried every single day. I decided to work on my clinical skills and earn some experience before thinking about attempting PLAB 2 again. — I joined RML Hospital as a Junior Resident in Accident and Emergency which led to the most amazing 5 months of my life. I learnt so much clinically, and in life. I developed my soft skills, my personality, confidence and made some great connections. This time was also filled with panic attacks and anxiety mid work thinking about my capability as a physician having failed PLAB 2. I was trying my best to brush off such thoughts, but I was only human. I would cry myself to sleep on some nights. Starting to journal was probably the best thing I did in 2023. Seeing my friends who had also failed during the ‘December PLAB 2’ period was probably more unsettling. Wondering each day, if we would ever make it. That failure was haunting me since the day I restarted my preparation for PLAB 2 in February ‘23. The fear had ginormously increased. No matter how much I would tell myself that I could do it, my fear always overpowered my confidence.. and I ended up crying every other day. My exam day was the last amongst my 2nd attempt friends. That allowed me to gain a lot of insight regarding small mistakes I shouldn’t be making during the exam. However, the fact that a mistake leading to a 0.5 lesser score could set me back, just like last time was horrifying. I didn’t want to be the only one left behind. Because that’s what it felt like. They couldn’t believe that Amrita could fail the exam she was so well suited for. Her speaking style, her knowledge, her skills. (PLAB 2 is an OSCE exam.) But it did happen.. and I now realise that it was OKAY. Sometimes we need to fail, to realise our potential. It taught me a lot about life and I will be forever grateful. Perhaps the most important lesson I learnt was to enjoy life as it comes. Things can turn any way, at any point of time. Your dreams will come true if you work on them. But your happiness will stay only if you let yourself feel it. From my exam day till my result day, I was anxious, crying, troubled. I couldn’t help but think negatively. I restarted journaling, and have been doing it till this day. It truly saved me from my own thoughts. I took one week medical leave before CGL mains. It burnt the _____ of my one senior. But I continued. My younger sister helped me so much during my struggling days. She made my dinner and packed my lunch for office so that I get time to study before and after office hours. Lessons learnt: Family is your strength. Nobody can take place of your family. Kitni hi achii dost kyu naa ho wo aapka khana nahi banayegi/banayega dusre city me aakar apna ghar chhodkar. My sister did this to help me excel in my exam. Give priority to your family. Return is good in this. Simple Maths. Help your parents, sisters, brothers. Be focused on your goal. APRIL 2023: Darshan to my lord Khatu Shyam ji🙏, Sikar. Personal life: My marriage got fixed to the same guy who stopped my parents from engaging me to him in February 2023. I had left the decision of my marriage completely on my parents and to my destiny. I got the hint on my very first meeting with the boy that God has planned this man. That is different story😊. MAY 2023: Gave Tier-II of SSC CPO 2022 because CGL 2022 result was not declared. By God's blessings and my parents’ wishes I got selected as PA in Department of Posts in SSC CGL 2022. Again it burnt the ____ of my one senior and many of my colleagues. I got sigh of relief although I didn't got my desired post but I was happy to see the happiness on my parents’ face. The senior was not happy with my success. He gave me dies non when I followed all the govt. rules. He showed me how power is misused to harass people. Lessons learnt: 1. Wishes and blessings works. Due to paucity of time, I know I didn't studied much (although i studied in whatever time i got. I dont used to waste even my single second.) but I got selected due to blessings of lord Krishna and little bit hardwork. Except your parents, spouse, sister and brother everybody will be jealous of your happiness. This is harsh reality. Logo ke muhh me meetha aur dil me chura🔪 hota hi, so always be alert. The same senior who harassed me used to say that I want you to succeed beta, May you get ASO in CGL. So be alert, people are so manipulative in Kalyug. JUNE 2023: My supportive senior said he will falsely take disciplinary action against me and will send file to the Department of post so that I don't get posting in my next office. I decided to resign from my job. I went to higher authorities for my resignation. Officials got shocked 😳 to hear my case. They remarked, you are a woman, why don't you complained? They changed my section means posting and supported me so much in my case. They dont wanted me to resign. Some officials treated me as if I am their daughter, they really loved me, cared for me. One old man in my office feed me with tea, biscuits, coffee, samosa, sweets. I started gaining weight🤣 which reflected during my engagement😁. Also went on a tour to Sawai Madhopur with my besties. Celebrated my papa's 50th birthday and gifted him his life's most expensive gift. 🎁 Lessons learnt: 1. As a woman, you must be aware and know the boundary, Act whenever is required. question_title: (2) How has 2023 been for you? - Quora
answer_text: Not good. Not as bad as 2022, but not exactly what I’d hoped for. I have gradually come to the realization over the past year that my life has been nothing but a string of very unwise decisions. Not only did this realization make 2023 more unpleasant in a general sense, but the consequences of those poor decisions came home to roost. And the earliest that I might be able to begin undoing the damage is late 2024. Granted, things seemed to be looking up in January. I interviewed for, and got, a job as an instructor at a flight school in Minnesota. Nothing I say hereafter should detract from that. I’m literally living the dream: flying for a living. Something I could scarcely have imagined in 2019, when I began attending flight school in Idaho. I started work in February, though, and life got tough again. Learning the ropes of a new job, a new career, and a new flight school (with its own idiosyncratic ways of doing things) was hard. The learning curve was steep. I discovered that I would start off my career as an instructor by teaching instrument flying, which was easier and safer than teaching brand-new student pilots, but had its own special challenges as well. The weather, also, was uncooperative. I moved to Duluth in the middle of one of the worst winters the city’s ever experienced. A cumulative 137 inches of snow, gale-force winds off Lake Superior, etc. My woefully underprepared Ford got stuck in the snow three times, and asking for my coworkers’ help was mortifying. Even as the months wore on and the weather became milder, other difficulties reared their ugly heads. I endured a four-month separation from my wife and daughter before I was able to bring them up to Duluth in June, and in the interim I lived in a house with some very nasty (and possibly mentally ill) housemates who made life unpleasant for me for several weeks. It was an improvement when my family was reunited, make no mistake—but we jumped the gun. I was in no shape to financially support three people on my salary, try as I might to supplement it by teaching courses at the local community college. My wife wasn’t able to get a job until November, and even then was reluctant to do so. She’s been pretty bitter about it, in fact—she seems to think that I promised her that she could be a stay-at-home mom once I started my flying career, and resents the fact that she’s had to rejoin the workforce. So in addition to our financial woes, the stress of juggling work schedules and picking our daughter up and dropping her off at daycare, the endless drudgery of working full-time and being full-time parents, and the daily trial of flight instructing, providing for my loved ones, and living hand-to-mouth, I’ve had to contend with my wife’s unspoken (and occasionally spoken) resentment. We don’t date, we don’t talk, our sex life is nonexistent, and things just haven’t been the same between us since early 2022. Apart from that, life’s just been hard in general. The daughter born to us in June of 2022 is now a toddler—a needy, noisy, messy toddler. Since she’s now going to daycare, the amount of sickness in our household has increased fivefold. The poor girl had dual earaches earlier this month, which made her a real treat to be around until the antibiotics took hold. Unfortunately, amoxicillin tends to cause diarrhea, so we’ve been laundering her bedding almost daily. My immune system is shot due to the immunosuppressants I’ve been on since 2016 for my ulcerative colitis, so I catch every single sniffle going around—and they linger for days, even weeks. I feel like I’ve been slightly sick for a month straight now. I was sick on my birthday and couldn’t take my parents (visiting from Idaho) flying. I had COVID again in November. I was sick on Christmas weekend, and between that and the acute pancreatitis my wife is having (as a result of the precipitous estrogen drop she experienced when she stopped taking her current birth control, which was giving her liver pain), we wound up skipping Christmas dinner altogether. Neither of us got any presents (except for a few books), as our funds are so tight that we told friends and family that we wouldn’t be exchanging gifts this year. All in all, it wasn’t the jolliest holiday. The last few Christmases and birthdays have been like that. The overarching theme you may notice whenever I write answers like this is money—or rather the lack of it, and the spirit-killing effect that it has on our lives. It relegates us to a very narrow range of activities, removes what little opportunity my wife and I have to date, and just generally depresses our mood. We’ve been living like this for far too long. And the worst part is that it’s our own fault. Mostly mine. (It'd be all too easy to blame things like “the system” or “’greedy corporations” or “capitalism” for our misfortunes, but only morons and losers do that.) We probably couldn’t have managed our finances worse if we tried. I’d paid off my student debt in Korea, but my wife’s debts are considerable, and we essentially doubled them when I decided to take out a loan and go to flight school. Then we bet the farm on me being hired by that same flight school when I’d completed my training, and we went ahead and conceived our daughter. Surprise: I wasn’t hired, leading to a desperate search for another position and thence to that debacle in Phoenix. This put us into an even worse financial hole, placed a permanent dent in my wife’s and my trust and respect for one another, caused me to fall back on the financial assistance of my parents (and readers like you) for the nth time, and increased my humiliation, depression, and discontentment a hundredfold. I’ve been so disgusted with myself that I told my wife and parents that I wanted neither cards nor gifts on Father’s Day 2023, nor even the slightest acknowledgement of the date. The consequences of our poor decisions are still being felt. My wife and I are still paying off the credit card debt we accrued during those awful eight days in Phoenix last year. We haven’t even been able to make any sort of headway in paying down our student debt. We’ve set ourselves back inestimably in the last few years. Our dreams of owning a B&B—or even just a goddamn house—have never seemed farther out of reach. We still have time, but I’m feeling my age. I turned 37 this year. How bitterly I regret not making smarter moves: eschewing a four-year university degree and the five-figure debt it incurred and going straight into flight school, for example. I could have had a house, a six-figure income, three kids, a dog, savings and retirement accounts, an investment portfolio, and thousands more hours of pilot-in-command time by now. But no. I had to do things the hard, slow, unpleasant way. Like I always do, apparently. 2024 might be the year it all finally begins to turn around. I should reach 1,000 hours of PIC time, and find a much higher-paying gig as a helicopter pilot in Duluth or elsewhere. (My wife and I aren’t at all sure where we want to live after this, or even whether we can afford to live anywhere else, which is another major source of uncertainty and discontentment in my life.) We should have our credit cards paid off, too. Our daughter Meryl will reach the age of two and a half, meaning she’ll attain the level of sophistication and articulateness required to more clearly convey her desires to my wife and me—and stop screaming in frustrated rage whenever we fail to understand what she wants. The sad mistakes of the last few years will finally be erased, in other words, and we can start all over again from a clean slate. Or so I hope. Now, you can murmur insipid platitudes like “at least you’re reunited with your family” and “you’ll get through this together,” as many of my friends and acquaintances (and even my parents!) have been doing. But it’s cold comfort. Call me a perfectionist, but I won’t breathe easy until I’m pulling down a salary commensurate with the lifestyle to which I believe we’re entitled at this point in our lives, and we start making some really concrete strides towards achieving our lofty goals of financial solvency and entrepreneurship.
author: Andrew T. Post

question_title: (2) How has 2023 been for you? - Quora
answer_text: 2023 has been quite strange for me. It is going to be almost one year now since I have started living in the United Kingdom. Since Feb, I have been living outside India, in a completely new environment, new culture, leaving behind all my friends and family. I left all my comforts of home to go and build my own world and create my identity as a doctor outside India. Anyone who has moved abroad will tell you- The first year is a strange one. Everything is new yet at the same time, everything is really hard. It takes time to adjust and us humans have these things called emotions which can be pretty harsh and brutal! Feb 23- August 23 The first three months were tough. UK is beautiful but it is also very lonely. Since you don’t have an established friend circle here, it becomes difficult to build those relations again. Especially when your 1–2 friends live in a different city or you are trapped in the swamp known as love! But I still did have some fun. I never stayed back home after work and went to city centre in Manchester and explored lot of different cuisines. Sat-Sun off and 9–5 Mon to Fri was something I never experienced before in India and this was really refreshing. I went roaming around in lot of cities as well with a friend who lives in London. Gloucester, London, Swansea, Mumbles, Newcastle etc. Some amazing street art and music as well in Manchester. York Ate some amazing food like every NRI will tell you- I learnt how to cook! Now I regularly make chicken, chole, rice, etc. Going to try biryani soon! September- December Now this is where you find another weird thing about UK. During the mid part of the year, days are really long. It would get dark at 9–9:30PM in May/June! And sunrise by 4AM from September though, you get shorter days and by December, it gets dark at 4PM and sunrise is by 8–8:30AM! It gets cold as well. Really depressing stuff sometimes. I would say by December, I adjusted well, got my own flat at rent without any sharing, I feel really happy that I can pay my own bills, buy my own stuff, get paid well and even save for future. I can’t tell you how much proud I felt when I sent 1k pounds (around a lakh) back home to mom when she needed it without any issue/sweat because I save more than that easily every month. Though my mom earns well herself (she is an amazing obstetrician and gynaecologist), I know that I can help her anytime with financial matters and that gives me relief. Of course, it is equally difficult to meet her and that can only happen once or twice an year. That’s the cost of living abroad. I also recently went through heartbreaks and breakup etc which are stories of another time. Trust me, these things don’t help lol when you are moving abroad and you have no friend support in face to face and you have to force yourself to be satisfied with online video calls which sometimes just are not enough! I even went to an anime con/comic con and it was spectacular! One amazing thing about UK is that they are really open about alcohol and you can get it anytime anywhere and quite at quite discounted prices in supermarkets. Really nice to see that much openness! Though of course, moderation is important. I also built a collection of fragrances! This is my new hobby. Many more to come in my collection! In the end, I would say that it has been a very happening year. Not the best though, but looking back, it has not been too bad unlike 2020 or 2021 where I lost some really precious people/things in my life. I won’t lie and say that going abroad is the best thing ever. It is not. It is good and you learn a LOT but it is difficult to adjust as well. Especially during the initial phase. I am still trying to make friends although I would say that fault is with me because I take time in trusting people and making true friend. But that will eventually happen. I am working in psychiatry, earn nicely, living on my own and hopefully will complete my training in this country. That is a good place to start! 2024, I hope you will be kind!

answer_text: Pretty unique, I must say. Why? Because I did something I had never done before in my life, i.e. an international trip, and that too solo. Just last week, I went to Turkey, to tour the cities of Istanbul and Antalya. What’s funny is that this was also the first time I’ve been on a flight, so I was kind of clueless of the entire boarding process, and given my anxiety, had a lot of questions brewing in my mind like, “What if I miss my flight (even though I reached the airport 3 hours before the scheduled departure)?”, or “What if they say that my tripod is a prohibited item and can’t be carried on a plane?” But then, a kind airport employee explained to me the entire process and answered all my queries, which relieved me of the stress I had and things went pretty well. I boarded the plane from New Delhi and when it went in the air, my ears got clogged and my head started hurting a little, something which I hadn’t expected to happen. It went away after a while but came back when we were landing in Istanbul but eventually subsided. I already had a ride booked to take me to the hotel, so I didn’t have to worry about looking for public transport. The driver was a pretty nice guy and although he spoke little English, but we managed to communicate. On my way, I kept looking outside for the most part and took pictures too. We even passed through a Roman Aqueduct and so that I could take a picture, the driver was kind enough to open the car’s sunroof, even without me asking him to do so. The Aqueduct of Valens, Istanbul I reached the hotel, took a shower, got dressed, and went on a stroll. I stayed in the Sultanahmet neighborhood where a lot of famous attractions are within walking distance. As I had already planned to see Hagia Sophia and other main monuments the next day, I decided to go see the Basilica Cistern: It’s a 6th-century underground cistern constructed during the reign of Byzantine Emperor Justinian I and served as a water filtration system for nearby buildings. Medusa, Basilica Cistern Medusa’s Head, Basilica Cistern The place has its own allure, even though it doesn’t get talked about as much as the Hagia Sophia or the Blue Mosque. The next place was The Topkapi Palace, which used to be the residence of Ottoman sultans, constructed on the orders of Mehmet the Conqueror, the guy who conquered Constantinople and ended the Roman Empire for good. After that, I just roamed around Sultanahmet Square and after some time, went back to the hotel. Later that day, I went for a Turkish bath appointment, and I gotta say boy, it was so good and relaxing!!! Even made my back and neck pain go away. My masseur asked me where I was from, to which I replied, “India”. He didn’t quite get it, so I remembered how they use the term “Hindi” for Indians. So, I said, “Hindi”. He responded with a smile, “Hindi! Indira Gandhi!!!” I replied, “Yeah, Indira Gandhi!” The next day I went to see the Grand Bazaar, Hagia Sophia, Blue Mosque, and the Hippodrome. Started with the Grand Bazaar, which is the world’s largest covered market, established back in Ottoman times: It has 61 streets in total. I, however, didn’t buy anything from there because, for one, I didn’t need anything, and second, the prices there are super inflated, especially given the fact that the rents of these shops are sky high. Third, the stuff sold there is, more often than not, a knockoff. To give you an analogy, if you’re an Indian living in or near Delhi, it’s like Palika Bazaar but way bigger. Then it was The Blue Mosque: It’s the only mosque in Istanbul with 6 minarets. Looks like this from the inside: You see those eggs hanging there? They’re actual ostrich eggs. It is believed that they repel spiders but there’s no scientific evidence to prove this claim. The next stop was Hagia Sophia: Being a history enthusiast, this was one of the main reasons why I visited Istanbul. It used to be a Byzantine church built under Justinian I, and when Mehmet conquered Constantinople and established Ottoman rule here, the building was converted to a mosque. Then, in 1935, Mustafa Kemal Ataturk, the founder of the Republic of Turkey, who also introduced many progressive reforms in the country, turned this building into a museum. And then, in 2020, Erdogan reversed that decision and now Hagia Sophia is once again a mosque. The interiors are also quite spectacular: I also saw those famous Byzantine murals: Then it was the Hippodrome, which used to have gladiator matches and later horse races during Roman times. Over there, there’s also this Egyptian Obelisk which was brought here by the Romans: It has other structures too, like the Serpent Column, The Fountain of Wilhelm II, etc. They used to have a lot more stuff here back in the Byzantine period but the Crusaders from Western Europe (Italy, France, etc), sacked Constantinople and took away a lot of things with them. Basically, the Crusaders pulled a British Museum on Constantinople (if you get the reference). In the evening, I decided to explore the city more, so I thought that maybe I should walk to the Galata Tower, and follow the directions given by Google Maps. Turned out to be a big mistake because I ended up getting lost and my feet were hurting badly. So, I chose to take a tram to a neighborhood named Kabatas and walk to the tower from there. The tower also overlooks a street named “Istiklal” which is famous for its nightlife and cafes: I walked around the street taking photos and then went to the nearest tram station to go back to the hotel. Then came the third day. Didn’t have much to do in the morning so went to the seafront, again by walking. Was windy as fuck but managed to get some good pictures. Also walked by what’s called “The Little Hagia Sophia”: In the evening, I went for a cruise through the Bosphorus, the strait that separates the European and the Asian parts of Istanbul. In this, you board a ferry and they take you on a two-and-a-half-hour cruise through the straight, explaining all the landmarks that you see on the way, including the history behind them. The above building was used as a hospital by Florence Nightingale during the Crimean War. It was quite windy during the cruise and the waves were very strong as well, which added to the experience, although given how I was taking photos while standing, I was afraid that either my phone, or I, or both, might fall into the sea, lol. The next day, it was time to say goodbye to Istanbul and fly to Antalya, which is a city situated on the Mediterranean coast. I arrived in the afternoon, and upon reaching the hotel, slept for a while. In the evening, didn’t have much to do, so asked the receptionist what could be done. So, he suggested a walk around the neighborhood, which was, not gonna lie, stunning. After returning from my walk, I just casually chatted with the receptionist, which eventually turned into a three-hour-long conversation on a sofa outside, mostly about history (lol!). He even brought me Turkish tea (They also call it “chai” just like us Indians. The only difference is that they don’t add milk). I was staying near Hadrian’s Gate, named after the Roman Emperor Hadrian, so I went there too: You can just walk through it, btw. The next day, I went on a guided city tour I had booked. Saw places like Duden Waterfalls: Did a Mediterranean boat trip: And also a cable car trip to the top of a hill. The third day in Antalya consisted of a full-day tour to Pamukkale, which is like 3 hours away from Antalya. Over there, I went to Lake Salda: It’s a crater lake that, along with its surroundings, is full of microbial fossils. These are some of the oldest known fossilized records of life on Earth. In 2021, NASA’s Perseverance rover reported that the rock and mineral deposits found in and around this lake are the closest match to those around the Jezero crater, where the rover had landed on Mars. The next stop was Pamukkale, which consists of large calcium deposits along with hot springs. Just next to Pamukkale, you have the ruins of Heirapolis, a Greco-Roman city. This place exists in an earthquake-prone zone, which led to it being destroyed and recreated several times until it was finally abandoned by the Romans (they learned their lesson). There were various magnificent structures like Cleopatra’s pool: (See those Roman pillars submerged in the pool?) The Temple of Pluto (the Roman equivalent of Hades): See that ditch below? They used to sacrifice bulls here. And even this Roman theatre: Spent quite a lot of time in Hierapolis because of how much this place has to offer, especially when you love history. And yes, I did make a lot of friends there too, something that is one of the biggest perks of traveling solo. This is Meining from London: Met her during the Antalya city tour when I happened to sit with her during lunch. We started talking about normal things like our itineraries, work, and others. Soon after that, we both realized we worked for the same company, the fact that we became friends over. Thus, we spent the rest of the day trip together. Also became friends with two Tunisian guys but sadly forgot to take photos with them. And yes, I’m still connected with each and every friend I made there. But it’s not that I only made human friends. I made a lot of furry friends as well. I mean, see for yourselves: And many more. Must easily have petted like 20–25 cats over there. A lot of them would just climb over me and start purring once I made the “pspspsps” sound and patted their heads. The cats in Turkey, especially in Istanbul, are super friendly. Turkish people are also very friendly, helpful, and kind, by the way. A lot of them also happen to be fans of Indian movies and actors like Aamir Khan and Alia Bhatt (for her role as Gangubai). I absolutely loved their hospitality, and how in many cases they went out of their way to help me. A lot of them were also quite curious and positive about my home country, India, something which I liked a lot. I loved every moment of my Turkey trip and I wish it were longer (a lot still remains to be explored, and thus, will definitely return someday). Hopefully, this is just the beginning of other solo international trips I may make in the future.
author: Parth Dutt

question_title: (2) How has 2023 been for you? - Quora
answer_text: Just few days left and it will be OVER! When I say over, I don't know what am I supposed to feel. This year wasn't easy on me, it really wasn't. I went through a phase, I never wanted to. Honestly, I would never want to experience an year as such again. You have had heard a lot of stories where people have failed in the first half but their sheer determination and “not giving up" attitude helped them in succeeding, but this year has been an episode of me giving up, because no amount of success was worth sacrificing my mental health for. The year started with me preparing for a ug competitive exam, I was preparing for the same from past 2 years and so. This year didn't marked the start of that journey but it surely did the end of it. Jan - May : Life wasn't easy. I was so done with that never ending preparation journey. Moreover, My health issues were at the peak, since I had insomnia and I've migraine issues too and these both can't go hand in hand. I also caught some infections because I wasn't myself completely to look after myself. True when they say, mental health issues starts reflecting on you physically. I gave my heart and soul to it, irrespective of the mess I had in my life. (You can see the pile of books at the left hand corner) In May, I gave my exam which was far better than how I expected it to be keeping everything in mind. It was the most toughest phase, I had in my life. I was on the verge of giving up, probably on life too. Nothing but proud of myself that I didn't let this thought overcome my will of living. June - Aug : Exam was done, result was announced and I was suggested to take one more drop by family, relatives, friends as they considered me so close to it, which probably was true. I was convinced when my mother said me the same but deep down I knew that I can't take all these again and I took the biggest leap of faith. I decided to quit. I, then, thought of doing graduation. I completely changed my stream as I wanted a fresh start with no nightmares of the thing I gave up on. And, I took admission in LPU, Jalandhar. Aug: Came to LPU not just with luggage but with baggage of a failure gifted by my relatives. Haha, it's funny how they taunt my parents for spending money on their daughter's education, it would be better if these taunts came on me not standing on my parent's expectations and not because I'm a girl but I can't help it out. Kudos to my parents for blocking out all those negativity and not letting me loose my self belief. Sept: I had my mid terms in September, they went pretty well except for accounts and I don't need to explain it. Oct: The highlights of October was Amritsar. The streets of Amritsar- The sunset- & lastly me in Golden temple - Nov: A Diwali away from home. Homesickness hits you more on such ocassions. The saddest part of November wasn't Diwali but chhath puja. People from Bihar could understand the pain of not being at home during chhath puja specially when your mother does the fast. Seeing her cry on video call, it's heart wrenching but then it was her decision that I shouldn't come as she was concerned about me travelling from Punjab to bihar considering my health issues. November, moreover, gave me life lessons. It taught me you can't just wear your heart on your sleeves in a world where people roam with knives in their hand. I feel blessed that I was always on the safer side but what I witness here is something that scares me of attachments more than ever. Dec: Currently giving my semester exams. 2023 was hard but a turning point in life. I went through failures, heartbreak, trust-breaks and a lot more. Things, people and situations made me emotionally numb, when I say I feel nothing emotionally, I mean it and I guess, it's better that way as now, I'm unbothered by people around. It's not that I'm suggesting everyone to be cold hearted or so, it's just that it works better for me that way and probably it's the best coping mechanism I discovered away from home where I can't just go and hug my mom to feel better. There are parts of this year that I didn't discussed above, probably because I don't wanna come out as someone gaining sympathy but at the end of the day it's not about how you went through but how you dealt with it and I guess, I did the best I could. I believe, It is better to be on the side of the sufferer than to be on the side of the perpetrator. Hoping that 2024 brings me a sense of accomplishment and be my year. A very happy and healing new year in advance to everyone reading this. May this year brings you everything you wish for. I hope you meet the healed version of yourself this year. People nearby can join me for coffee on new year. Thankyou:) Happy reading:)
